sacrilegium.c: SACRILEGIUM, Sacrilege, or an Alienation to Lay-men, and to profane or common purposes, of what was given to Religious Persons, and to I ions Uses. sacrumof.c: SACRUM Of : The Os Sacrum is the broadest of all the Bones of the Back, and doth sustain all the other Vertebra .- On the inside it is smooth and hollow, on the outside convex and uneven, being of something a triangular shape. In its upper part on each side it is knit firmly to the Ojfa Ilia, by an inverting Cartilage. It consists of five or six Bones, plainly distinguishable in Infants,but more obscurely in grown Persons. These Bones have the Resemblance of (and are usually called) Vertehr.e ; for each of them hath a Body and Processes, and a large hole to receive the Spinalis Medulla . The Bodies of these differ from those of the other Vertebr.c in this respect ; that whereas in those the lower part is always bigger, in these it is the less; by which means the uppermost is the biggest, and the lowest the least. Their smaller holes which serve for the ingress and egress of the Vessels, differ also from those of the other, in that they are not in their sides, but before and behind ; of which those les axe are much the large*. A* forth air Processes, the Oblique can hardly be discerned, except in t'^ first. The Transverse arc pretty long, but 1° unl> ted, that all seem but one. saliva.c: SALIVA, or Spittle, is a Liquor separated by proper Ducts (which they call the Dudus Salivates) from the Glands of the Mouth, as the Parotides, the Glandule Nudiamc, the Maxillares, the Subtingualcs. ‘Tis probable that the Origin of tire Saliva, is from the Arterious Blood ; for as the Arteries pour Nutritious Blood into all other parts, so they do into the Glands also ; part of which they convert into their own Nourishment, part is returned by the Veins in the circulation, and part (vi%. of what is serous) they separate, and bestowing a subacid quality thereupon, makes aliva (or Spittle) of it. To the Composition whereof (if not for the Separation of it) seme think a Nervous Juice is contributed, the rather because larger and more numerous Twigs of Nerves are communicated to the Glands, then to more other parts, which yet have a more exquisite sense then these. But in refutation of this Opinion, the abovementioned Dr. Nuck alledges this Experiment : That if the Nerve that runs to any Gland, be either hard tied or cut in sunder, yet the Secretion of the Saliva will not thereupon cease, but will only proceed more slowly ; which slowness may be attributed not to the want of any constitutive Principle of the Saliva, so much as to the want of that Motion in the Gland (that to be sure depends as well upon the Nerve aS upon the Pulsation of the Artery) which is necessary for the quicker dispatch of the Saliva, through or out of the Gland. The manner of the Secretion of the Saliva, is like that of the Liquor of all other Glands, and proceeds from the Conformity of the Particles of the Liquor to the Pores in the Gland, or the Mouths of the Excretory Vessel. After its Separation, its Motion into and along the Salival Ducts, is much farthered by the Muscular Motion of each part respectively. Now the Saliva is not to be reputed a mccr Excrement, for it is believed by all Modern Anat )- mists, that it serves for the farthering of the Fermentation of Meats in the Stomach, if it be not the main Ferment of it. That it has a fermentative Quality Diemcrbroeck proves by this Experiment: That if a piece of white Bread be chewed and moisten’d with much Spittle,and then be mixed with Wheat-paste kneeded with warm Water, it will make it ferment. Dr. Pluck thinks it is an Universal Ferment for Meats and Drinks, partaking of divers Qualities (or Particles) but of none in any excessive Degree. That it is acid he demonstrates by this familiar Observation. " That if when Milk is a boiling, one take a “ Spoonful to taste ot, and then presently whilst it “ is moist Saith the Saliva, put it into the Milk a- " gain (still a boiling) the Milk will break as if “ some acid Liquor were mixed with it. Thar it is endued with a Volatile Salt, he thinks is evident from its curing the Itch, 1 otters, (3c. That Oleous Particles are mixed with the acid, he supposes must be concluded from its killing Quicksilver : And whereas it usually becomes frothy in the Mouth, upon its being agitated by the Motion of the Muscles of the Tongue, and those which move the lower Jaw, and that he thinks proceeds from its being endued with a Lixivial Salt and Spiritous,Oleous and acid Particles,(while the Volatile Spirit vanishes.) 6 K z SAL ISAP SAL

salt.c: SALT, the first of the three Hypostatical, but the third of the live Chymical Principles: Its two Essential Properties seem to be, Dijsolubility in Water, and a petty Pungent Sapor, being an active incombustible Substance ; they say it gives all Bodies their Consistence, and preserves them from Corruption, and occasions all the Variety of Tasts. There are three Kinds of Salts: Six J, Volatile, and Essential. The Six’d Salt is thus drawn : The Matter is first calcined, and then the Allies are boil’d in a good deal of Water, that the Salt may be the better dislblved: After this the Solution is filtrated, and all the Moisture evaporated, and then the Salt remains in a dry form at the bottom of the Vessel. This Six’d Salt so drawn, is called a Lixivious Salt, because a kind of Lixivium, or Lye, was made of the Ashes of the Body calcined. Volatile Salt, is that which is drawn from the Bodies or Parts (chiefly) of Animals, and from some fermented, or rather putrified parts of Vegetables: It rises quick and easily, and is the mest Volatile of any Bodies so called. The essential Salt is drawn from the Juice of Plants by Chrystallization : How, see Essential Salt. Mr. Boyle reckons three other Kinds of Salts, viz. Add, Vrinous, and Lixiviate: Sec those Words. And he discovers whether any Liquor contains an Add Salt, or no, by dropping some of it on Syrup of Violets, for then it will turn it red ; but if it turn it green, it is either of an Vrinous or Lixiviate Nature: To distinguish which, he drops some of it into a Solution of Sublimate made in common Water ; then if a white or milky colour be produced, he concludes it to belong to the Tribe of Vrinous Salts ; but if it produce a yellow or orange colour, he judges it to be of a Lixiviate Nature.

saltofsaturn.c: SALT of Saturn, Saccharum Saturni, or Sugar of Lead, is the Body of that Metal opened and reduced to the Form of a Salt by distilled Vinegar. Thus any of the Calxes of Lead, as Pappose Ceruse, is powdered, and distilled Vinegar is poured upon it to four Fingers height above the Matter, an Ebullition will follow, but without sensible heat it must be digested in a Sand-heat, two or three Days, and stirred often : Then pour oss the Liquor by Inclination, and digest more distilled Vinegar with the Ccrit/e, and more after that, till you have dissolved about half the Matter, mix all the Impregnations together in an Earthen or Glass Vcllel ; evaporate the Matter in a Sand-heat, till a small Skin or Pellicle, begin to arise upon the Surface; after which, place the Vessel in a cool place, there will appear white Crystals: Take them out, and evaporate again as before, and set the Vessel to cool to gain the rest of the Salt: Continue this till you have gotten all ; then dry the Crystals in the Sun, and keep them in a Glass. ’Tis chiefly used out-. war div for Diseases of the Skin; but sometimes tis given inwardly, from two to four Grains at a Dole in Quinsies, (3 c.

Saturn’s Year is almost 30 of ours, but the length of his Day is yet uncertain, because the time of his Revolution round his Axis is not yet known : But Mr. Uugcns judges they are not longer than the Days in Jupiter. That great Astronomer supposed the Axis of Saturn to be perpendicular to the Plane of his Ring, and of the Orbits of the Satellites: If so, then there will be the same Position of the Equator and Poles, (as to the Fixt Stars) as there is in our Earth : The same Pole Star and the Fixt Stars will appear to Rile and Set after the same manner, in the lame Latitudes. There is a vast Inequality in the Length of the Day in several parts of this Planet ; and as great a diversity of Summer and Winter ; which depends on the Quantity of the Inclination of the Plane of the Equator, to the Plane of the Orbit of Saturn round the Sun ; which Hugcijs makes to be 31 Legr. which is almost -] more than in our Earth; where yet the differences and variety of Seasons and Weather are very sensible. For in Saturn, in the Lapitudc of 50 Dcgr. the longest Day will have no Night at all, and the longest Night will have no Day. And the two Frigid Zones will be each of them 62 gr. broad, at least 1 o times as large as the whole Surface of our Earth. The Eye thus placed, will be able to discern none of the Planets but Jupiter, which will appear always to accompany the Sun, and never to be from him above 37 gr. The Parallax of the Sun in Saturn, is but 9", and therefore Insensible; but the Parallaxes cf all his Moons or Satellites, arc very considerable, and therefore their Distances from him will be easily computable. But what an Eye placed in Saturn would most admire, is the Ring of that Planet; the finly thing of that nature that is discovered in any of the Planets. The. Kepler in his Epitome Aftron. Cepernic. Lib. 4. p. 586, and after him Capt. I!alley in his Enquiry into the Causes of Variation of the Needles Variation, Phil. Trans. N° 195, do suppose our Earth may be composed of several Crusts or Shells one within another, and concentrical to each other. And if so, then ’tis possible the King of Saturn may be the fragment or remaining Ruins of his formerly exterior Shell, the rest of which is broken and fallen down upon the Body of the Planet. And if Saturn ever had such a Shell round it, its Diameter would then have appeared as big to an Eye at the Sun, as that of Jupiter doth now, when seen from thence. Since the outward Margin of the Ring is distant from Saturn 2 { of Saturn's Semidiametcr, this cannot be seen at the distance of 64 Dcgr. from Saturn's Equator (in whose Plane the Ring is placed) Therefore a Spectator placed in a Latitude higher than that, can never see the Ring at all; so that there is a Zone of almost 5 3 0 broad toward either Pole, to whom this famous Ring can never appear. And as the Spectator shall move nearer the Pole, first one, then the second Satellite, next die third and fourth ; and when he is come within one Degree of the Pole, even the fifth Satellite cannot be seen, unless by Pefraction; and in the V inner-time, neither, Sun, Moon, or any Planet, will be there visible, unless perhaps a Comet. If the Eye be supposed to be placed in the Equator of Saturn, or in the Zone nearly adjoining, it can never fee those Stars that are in or very near the Equator, nor any one of the Satellites ; because the Ring will always hide them ; and then at the Equinoxes it cannot fee the Sun ; and if it were any where

S All S C A where else placed, it ecu Id r.ot then lee the Ring • because neither otites Faces will then appear illuminated by the Sun. The Breadth of this Ring *ris hard to determine from our Earth, because its Thickness is so small: But Mr. Hugens makes it bo be about six hundred German Miles. For one half of Saturn's Year, (viq. 15 Years of ours) only one Face of the Ring will be enlightened by the Sun: Whence the Inhabitants which may be supposed to Live in that Hemisphere, to which this Face of the King is turned, or to whom it is Summer, w.iil fee that part of the Ring which is above their Horizon, shining faintly by Day, (as our Moon doth when the Sun is above our Honzon) but brighter and stronger by Night, as our Moon doth in the Sun’s absence : And after Sun-fer, the Eaitern part of this enlightened Arch will fall within the Shadow of Saturn ; which Shade will ascend as Night comes on, and at Midnight wilt be ar the highest ; and then will descend again towards the Western part of the Ring, according as the Sun comes more and more to the Eastward. . This enlightened Ark will always strew how to describe a Meridian Line; for a Plane perpendicular to the Horizon, and pa ing thorough the Vertex of the Ark, will be in the true Meridian. To an Eye placed any where without, and at less than 51* distance from the Equator, this enlightened Ark of die Ring will appear Concave as well as Convex, like a kind of Furnace or Vault, riling above the Horizon : But to an Eye at more than 52', and less than 64 Degrees distant from the Equator, she hollow or concave Bart will not be visible; but there wijl appear a brighristi Body arising as it were out of the Ground, aud contiguous to the Horizon. For the other half of Saturn’s Year, while the Sun declines towards the depressed bole, or during the 1 5 Years Winter, the Ring will not be visible, as having not that Face Illuminated which is obverted to the Spectator’s Eye ; but however, will render it self sensible, by covering from the Sight, such Stars and Parts of the Heavens as arc opposite to it, or apparently behind it. The Shade of the Ring also will be extended more and more towards the nearer Pole; so that to an Eye placed any where within the aforesaid space, the Sun, when he attains such a certain Declination, will appear to be covered or eclipsed just at Noon, and then strait to emerge out of the Shadow. The next Day, the like Phxnomenon will happen, but the Eclipse will begin sooner, and will be over later : And these Meridian Eclipses will daily cncreaie in their duration, until the middle of Winter ; and then they will decrease again gradually, till at last they will come to nothing again ; vi% When the Sun returning from the Tropick, hath the lame Declination as lie had when these Meridional Eclipses began. And this will happen, if any Eye be placed in any Latitude greater than 25 or 26 Degrees; but if in a Latitude less than this, when the Meridian Darkness is of the greatest duration, the Sun will suddenly appear just in the Meridian, and then il railway will be Eclipsed again. The next Day, there will appear the like sort of I.sight, but it will last longer; and this Meridian Light will grow still longer and longer in duration, till Midwinter, and then (like the Darkness above-mentioned) it will be continually decreasing, until it quite disappear. .— ■ - I- --.—----- [jC And from hence ’ris plain, that there is greatest difference between Summer and V' inter , the Globe of Saturn, of all the other Planets; this both on the account of the long duration each, and the great declination of the Sun r , the Equator; and also,by reason of these Verso 101 '. scaleofthegamut.c: SCALE of the Gamut, or Musical Scale, is a kind of Diagram, consisting of certain Lines and Spaces drawn to thew the several Degrees, whereby a Natural or Artificial Voice or Sound may either ascend or descend. The Name thereof is taken from the Greek ’ Letter Gamma, which Guido Aretinus, who reduced the Greek. Scale into this Form, plac’d at the bottom, to signifie from whence it was derived; so that ever since, this Scale or Gammut, hath been taken for the Ground-work or first Foundation of all Mustek, both Vocal and Instrumental. But there were three different Scales in use among the Ancients, which had their Denominations from the three several sorts of Mustek, vi\. The Diatonical, Chromatical, and Enharmonical. Which see.

scaleni.c: SCALENI, are three Muscles of the Thorax, so called from their Figure, having three unequal Sides. 1. Its Use is to draw the superior Rib, together with the rest, upwards in Inspiration. i. Scalenus Secundus, this springs fleshy from the second, third, fourth, and fifth Transverse Processes of the Vertebra of the Neck, laterally, (like the former j in its descent, it becomes thin and tendinous, marching over the first Rib to its Insertion in the second, and sometimes to the third. 3. Scalenus Tertius, this has its beginning near the former, from the same Transverse Processes of the Vertebra. of the Neck • as also from the fifth and sixth of those Processes, and is soon Inserted to the first Rib.

secretion.c: SECRETION, is the separation of one Fluid from another in the Body ot an Animal or Vegetable, by the means of Glands or something analogous to them. Dr. Havers in his Osteologia, explains Glandular Secretion, by observing, first, That all Motion in its proper Tendency is direct, (which is exactly right) and that the Glands which are feared on the (ides of the Arteries all over the Body, are so placed, as to. favour the motion of any Particles that strike against them in a right Line, more than the Veins; and having Pores adapted to the Figure of the Particles which they separate, the Particles endeavour in their motion to get into thole Glandules; and being there received, are separated and distinguished from the rest of the mass of Blood, and so assume the form of that Liquor which we find separated by every Gland. And that the Glands are so situated as to favour the motion of a Particle in a right Line more than the Veins, he faith, is apparent from Observation of the gradual construction of the Arterial Channel. sectionconick.c:
SECTION Conick,, is the Figure made by the solidity of a Cone’s being supposed to be cut by a Plane. If the Se El ion be made by the Axis, or through the Vertex, the Figure arising is a Triangle. If by a Plane, parallel to the Base of the Cone,or subcontrari/y posited, the Figure produced is a Circle. If the Sell ion be made parallel to one side of the Cone, the Figure produced is a Parabola If thro' both sides of the Cone, 'tis an El iff s ; and if thro’ one side of the Cone, thro’ the Base, and not parallel to the other side of the Cone, ’tis an Hyferbola. Archimedes, Euclide, and other ancient Mathematicians, called that only a ConicliSethon, when the Plane cutting the Cone was at right Angles to the side of the Cone ; and according as the Angle made by the sides of the Cone meeting in the Vertex, as it was a right, obtuse, or acute one, they called it the v action of Rigbt-angled, Obtuse-angled, Or Acute-angled Cone. By which Words they understood what we now call the Parabola, the Hyferbola, and the Elifsis : Which three Sections, fas also the Circle) Afolonius Pergatus (justly called Magns

S b c S E G Magnus Geometra) found our to be producible in any Cone, according to the four ways of cutting it, as above-mentioned. .SECTION, in Mathematick, signifies the cutting of one Plane by another, or a Solid by a Plane. The common Ser ion of two Planes is always a right Line, being the Line supposed to be drawn on one Plane by the Section of the other, yr by its Entrance into it.

SF.RRATUS Major Anticus, is a Muscle which r “ es fleshy from the whole Basts Scapula:, and pasS E R sing under the Sulfcapularis, it becomes broader and thicker, still running somewhat forwards till it’s inserted to the eight superior Ribs laterally, by so many distinct Fleshy Portion', or Digital:, representing the Teeth of a Saw; the two, and sometimes three inferior of which, are indented with the Mustulus Obltquus Defccndens of the Avdomen. This like the Serratus Minor Anticus, dilates the Thorax, or moves the Scapula: forwards and downwards, when its Muscles arc relax’d. SERRAI US Minor Anticus, is a Muscle, by Anatomists generally reckoned a Muscle amongst those of the Scapula ; but we are perswaded 1 says Cowper) from its Position that it may be equally serviceable to the Thorax, in elevating those Ribs it is inserted to: It arises fleshy from the Proceisus Coracoides Scapula, and descends obliquely forwards, becomes broader and thinner, and is inserted fleshy to the bony part of the second, third, fourth, and fifth Ribs. If the Scapulae are elevated by their proper Muscles, this with its Partner, are then capable of dilating the Breast in large Inspirations. serratusinferiorpofiicus.c: SERRATUS inferior pofiicus, is a Muscle of the Thorax, much larger than Authors generally assign it: “ In a Robust Man we observed its Continu- “ ation, (lays Cowper) not only from the Spines of " the Vertebra's of the Loins, but from all those of “ the Thorax, as well underneath as below the for- “ mer Muscle ; its superior and inferior Parts be- " ing entirely Tendinous, its Middle growing “ fleshy near its serrated Termination at the Cur- “ va ture of the ninth, tenth,eleventh, and Extremi- “ ty of the twelfth Ribs. The Ductus of the Fibres “ of this palling transverse, and those of the precc- " dent descending obliquely, do decussate each o- " other in acute Angles j which Isolan has well ob- “ served, and contrary to the Opinion of Authors, “ assigns it with its Partner, a different Use in det‘ pressing the Thorax ; both performing the Office " of a Bandage in binding together and constringing “ the Posterior Muscles of the Spine, not unlike the “ Constructive Inclosures of the Thigh and Cu- “ bit.

serratussuperiorpoflicus.c: SERRATUS superior poflicus, is a Muscle of the Thorax, which lies immediately under the Rjjoniboides : It arises witsi a thin Tendon from two inferior Spines of tlse Vertebra of the Neck, and three superior of the Thorax, from thence descending obliquely over the Splenius Capita, and under parts of the Sacrolumbalis, and Dorst Lpngijstmus, it becomes fleshy, marching under the Scapula, to its Insertion at the Curvature of the second, third, and fourth Ribs, by so many distinct fleshy endings, representing the Teeth of a Saw, whence its Name. SEXAGESIMAL Fraiiions, or Sexagenaries, are such as have always 60 for their Denominator: There were antiently no others used in Astronomical Operations; and they are still retained in man J Cases ; tita* Decimal Arithmetics begins to groW in Use now in Astronomical Calculations. In these Fractions, which some call Aflronorm - cals) the Denominator is usually omitted, and the Numerator only written down : Thus. 4 % 59 ', 32 .”, 5 °'", Is to be read, 4 Degrees, 5 9 Minutes, 32 Seconds of a Degree, or 60th parts of a Minute, 50 Thirds, 16 Fourths, £ 3 v. The Ancients, before the introducing of Algorism by the Numeral Figures now in use, (finding, it troublesome to express and manage Fractions ot divers Denominators, especially when they are to be expressed by great Numbers ; and troublesome also to express and manage Integers, when thef happen to be great Numbers) thought fit to divide an Integer into 60 Parts, which they call’d asYIq which now we call Minutes, or Scruples ; and each of these into 60 Parts, which they called Seconds, and (if there were yet need of greater Exactness) each of these into 60 Thirds; and each ot these into as many Fourths; and so onward, as far as there were occasion, which they called Sexagefms, or Sexagcssimal parts. - And (to avoid great Numbers) a Collection ot sixty Integers they called a Sexagcne ; and sixty of such, a Second Sexagcne ; and sixty of these, a Third 3 and so onward, as there was occasion. Thus, for J, the fourth part of an Integer, (b e it Hour, Day, Degree, or whatever else) they p 1 ^ 1 '5 s (that is, 15 Minutes); for 4, they put 7'. 3 ° ' (that is, 7 Minutes and 30 Seconds); which is exactly the same in Value : And for 4,) because this cannot be exactly express’d in Scxagcfms) die/ would put 8 s , (which is pretty near, but somewhat too little) or 9' (which is yet nearer, but somewhat too much) or (if these be not exact enough for th® present purpose) 8 34", or 8 r 34" 17 s " ; or y^ c more accurately, if need be, till they come to 0 much exactness, as that the small remaining difference might safely be neglected. smelling.c: SMELLING, is ppobably occasioned by the Effluvia of Odorous Bodies mingling themselves with the Air, and cutting up the Nostrils, which arc covered with a very Nervous and Sensible Coat, and there insinuating themselves into the Processes of the Olfactory Nerve, do move it variously according to their various and different Nature, and so communicate to the Brain, such corresponding Motions, as enables the Soul to judge differently of the Bodies emitting such Effluvia : And from hence when the Effluvia produces a grateful Sensation, we say it hath a sweet Smell, but when a disagreeable one, we say it stinks. SMITEING-Line, in a Ship, is a small Rope fastned to the Misscn-YardfArm, below at the Deck, and is alway furled up with the Missen-fail, even to the upper end of the Yard, and from thence it comes down to the Poope. Its Use is to loose the Missen-fail without striking down the Yard, which is easily done, because the Missen-sail is furled up only with Rope-yarns; and therefore when this Rope is pulled hard, it breaks all the Ropeyarns, and so the Sail falls down of it self: The Word of Art is, Smite the Mijfcn (whence this Rope takes its Name ;) that is, hale by this Rope that the Sail may fall down.

This ready Block is commonly fastened with a Strap about the Main-mast, close to the Upper Deck, and is chiefly used for the Fall of the Winding Tackle, which is reeved into this Block, and then brought to the-Capstan.

snow.c:
SNOW. The Learned Dif. Grew, in Philosophical Transactions, N. 92. gives the following Account of Snow, which seems very exact and just. 6 N 1. With

S N O SNO 1. With Mr. Des Crf)-t«,and DrJioo 4 ,he observes* That many parts hereof arc of a Regular Figure; for the most: part being as it were so many little Rowels, or Stars of 6 Points; being perfect and transparent Ice, as any one may fee upon a Pool, or Velselol Water; upon each of which 6 Points, are set other collateral Points, and those always at the same Angles, as are the main Points themselves. 2. Amongst these Regular Figures, tho’ many of them arc large and fair; yet from these taking our first Item, many others, alike Regular, but far less, may likewise be discovered, 3. Amongst these, not only Regular, but entire Parts of SnOW, looking still more warily, we shall perceive, that there are divers others indeed irres ular, which yet are chiefly the broken Points, arcels, and Fragments of the Regular ones. 4. That besides the broken parts, there are some others which seem to have lost their Regularity, hot so much in being broken, as by various Winds, first gently Thaw’d, and then Froze into little irregular Clumpers again. From whence the true Notion, and external Nature of Snow, seemeth to appear, ,vi%. That not only some few parts of Snow, but originally, the whole Body of it, or of a Snowy Cloud, is an infinite Mass of Icicles regularly figured ; not one Particle thereof, I say, originally, not one of so many Millions,; being indetermined, or irregular: That is to say, a Cloud of Vapours being gathered into Drops, the laid Drops forthwith descend ; upon which Descent, meeting with a soft freezing Wind, or at least passing thro’ a Colder Region of the Air, each Drop is immediately froze into an Icicle, Shooting it self forth into several Points or StirLc, on each Hand frontward,its Center : But still continuing their descent, and meeting with some sprinkling and intermixing Gales of Warmer Air, or in their continual Motion and Wastage to and fro, touching upon each other; some are a little thaw’d, blunted, frosted, clurnpcr’d, others broken, but the most hanked and clung in several Parcels together, which we call Flanks of Snow. It being known what Snow is, we understand, why, though it seem to be soft, yet ’tis truly hard ; because true Ice, the inseparable property whereof is to be hard ; seeming only to be soft, because upon the first touch of the Finger, upon any of its sharp Edges or Points, they instantly thaw ; or 0ther wise they would pierce our Fingers as so many Lancets. Why again, though Snow be true sty, and so hard and dense a Body, yet very light; because of the extream thinness of each Icicle in comparison of its breath. For so Gold, which though of all Bodies it be the most ponderous, yet being beaten into Leaves, rides upon the least breath of Air ; and so in all other Bodies, where there is but little Matter contained within large Dimensions, and possibly in no other Cafe. Also, how it is HSjitc, not because hard ; for there are many soft Bodies White ; but because consisting of parts, all of them singly transparent, but being mixed together appear White; as the Parts of Froth, Glass, Ice, aud other transparent Bodies, whether soft or hard. Thus much for the External Nature of Snow ; let us next enquire into its Ejjential Nature. solstice.c: SOLSTICE, is the Time when the Sun entring the Tropical Points, is got furthest from the Equator, and before he returns back towards it, seems to be for some time at a stand, being moved in the same Parallel, and scarce making any other Lines than perfect Circles, so small is its Progress. These Solstices are two : Estiva!, or Summer Solstice, when the Sun enters Cancer the 11 th of June, making the longest Day, and the shortest Night. And the Hyemal, or Winter Solstice, on the 11 th of December, when he enters Capricorn, the Nights being then at the longest, and Days at the shortest ; that is, in Northern Regions, for under the Equator there is no Variation, but a continual Equinox; and in the Southern Parts, the Sun's Entrance into Capricorn, makes the longest Day ; and into Cancer, the longest Night.

sound.c:
SOUND, seems to be produced by the subtil cr, and more Etherial Parts of the Air, being formed and modified into a great many small Masses or Contextures, exactly similar in Figure ; which Contextures are made by the Collision and peculiar Motion of the Sonorous Body, and flying off from it, arc diffused all around in the Medium, and there do affect the Organ of our Ear in one and the same manner. Sound, also appears not to be produced in the Air, so much by the swiftness, as by the very frequent Repercussions, and reciprocal Shakings of the Sonorous Body. Mr. Isaac Newton demonstrates, (in Prop. 43. Lib. i. of his Principles ;) That Sounds, because they arise from the Tremulous Motion of Bodies, are nothing else but the Propagation of the Pulse of the Air. And this he faith, is confirmed by those great Tremors that strong and grave Sounds excite in Bodies round about, as the Ringing of Bells, noise of Cannon, (fc. And in another place he concludes, That Sounds do not consist in the Motion of any Æther, or finer Air, but in the Agitation of the whole common Air; because he found by Experiments, That the Motion of Sound depended on the Density of the whole Air. He found by good Experiments, That a Sound moves 968 Feet, English, in a Second of Time, rag.370. Supposing the Air, by the Pulse which causes Sound, to be in a Motion, like that of the Water when its Waves roul; he calculates the Breadth of the Pulse, or the Distance between Wave and Wave, to be in the Sounds of all open Pipes, double the Length of those Pipes, which he grounds on an Experiment of Father Mersennus , in hisHat' monicks, that an extended String made 104 Vibrt' tiont in a Second, when it was an Undone wst* 1 the C, fa, Vt Pipe of an Organ, whose Length was 4 Foot open, and 2 Foot stop’d, pag. 37a. Why the Sound ceases always with the Motion of the Sonorous Body; and why they reach th c Ear equally soon, when far off, or near : Helhews in Prop. 48. Cor. where he proves, That the Nit®' ber of the Pulses propagated, is always the very same with . the Number of the Vibrations ot the Tremulous Body, and that they are not by at>y means multiplied as they go from it. The following Properties have been observed $ Sound ; in many of which, there is a near dp’ lation between it and Light. For, 1. As Light acquaints the Eye with the di# c ' rent Qualities, Magnitudes, and Figures of Asdics, so Sound in like manner informs the Ear oJ many of the same Things, in the Sonorous Body2. A greater Sound drowns a less, as a grea tcf Light Eeclipses a less. 5 Too Great,Loud,or Shrill a Sound is Offenses and Injurious to the Ear, as too great and bright * Light is to the Eye. 6 . Sound also (like Light) moves sensibly b -0 / 11 Place to Place, tho’ no thin g near so swift as It is Reflected like Light from all hard Bodies; ' is hindred and refracted, by pasting thro’ a Dei" Medium. But it differs from Light in this, (h a whereas Light is always propagated in ■R.sigh' Lines, the Motion of Sound is almost always Curvilinear. 7. As to Reflexion of Sounds: ’Tis observe^ that if one stand near the Reflecting Body, a j’ c the Sound be not very farr off, tho’ an Eccho produced, yet it cannot be heard; because ths ^ rect and Reflex Sound, enter the Ear almost ^ the same time : But then the Sound appears to stronger than ordinary, and lasts longer: Efp cCI . s ly when the Reflexion is made from divers B° c

specifickgravity.c:
SPECIFICK Gravity, is the Appropriate aud peculiar Gravity or Weight, which any Species of Natural Bodies have, and by which they are Plainly Distinguishable from all other Bodies of Different kinds. By some ’tis not improperly called Relative Gravity, to distinguish it from Absolute Gravity, which cncreases in Proportion to the Bigness of the Body weighed. Thus if any Body weigh a Pound, one as big agen will Weigh two Pounds: and let the Bodies be of what Nature or Degree of Specifick Gravity soever, a Pound of one will be as much as a Pound of the other Absolutely considered : Thus, as is commonly said, a Pound of Feathers, is as heavy as a Pound of Lead. But if you consider Lead and Feathers Relatively, the Specifick Gravity of the Former, will be much greater than that of the Latter. Or Lead, or Bulk, for Bulk will be much heavier than Feathers : And Gold heavier than Lead, Lse. ’Tis of so great Advantage in many respects as will appear below to find truly the Specifick Gravities of Bodies, that many Curious Ways have been thought of, and experimented for this Purpose. As by forming exact Cubes of different substances, and taking their Weight accurately in Nice Scales ; and by melting Metals of different Gravities, and then casting them in Molds of the same Dimensions. But for Practice and Universal use, nothing is better than the following Method, which is to weigh any Body first in Air, and then in Water ; which latter being considerably a Denser Fluid than Air, will buoy up the Body immersed in it in part; and will consequently make it weigh less there than in the Air. And if after this you substract the Weight found in the Water, from the former in the Air; a Remainder or Difference will be sound, which is the Weight of as much Water as is equal to the Bulk of the Body. As Archimedes hath demonstrated Mathematically, and Mr. Boyl Physically and Experimentally, in his Ilydroftical Paradoxes. So that by this means having two Bodies, one Firm, and the other Liquid, with the Weight of each apart; "tis very easy to find the Proportion that one hath to the oS P E S P E ther, Bulk for Bulk; by only dividing the greater by the lesser ; for then the Quotient will Ihew the Specifick Gravity of the Heavier Body compared with as much Warcr as is equal to it in Bulk. As if the Quotient be z, 3, 6, or 19; the Body will accordingly be twice, thrice, 6, or 19 times as heavy as Common W water. spermatidveiiels.c: SPERM ATI d VeJJels, and Parts, arc those Arteries and Veins, which bring the Blood to, and convey ir from the Testicles: Likewise those Vessels through which the Seed passes: Likewise all whitish Parts of the Body, which because of their C stout, were Anciently thought to be made of the Seed : Of this sort are the Nerves, Bones, Membranes, Gristles; &c.

spermatocele.c: SPERMATOCELE, a Rupture caused by the Contraction of the Vessels which eject the Seed, and its falling down into into the Scrotum.

sphacelus.c: SPHACELUS, is a sudden Extinction of Life and sense in every Part. SPHÆNOIDAL 1 S Sutura, is a Suture that surrounds the Os SpLcnoidcs, seperates it from rhe Os Occipitis, from the Os Petrosta, and from the Os Frontis,

sphnoides.c: SPHÆNOIDES, is a Bone of the Cranium, common bothHO the Skull and upper Jaw ; it is of a very irregular Figure; and is situated in the middle of the Basis of the Skull, and is joyned to all the Bones of the Cranium, by the Sutura Spbatnoidalis, except in the middle of its Sides, where ir is continued to the Ossa Petrosa as if they were one Bone. This Bone has a small Protuberance in the Middle thereof, from which the Muscles of the ZJvula arise: On its Inside it has four Processes called Clinoides. Betwixt the two Tables of this Bone, under the Cell a Turica, there is a Sinus divided in two in the Middle, which opens by two Holes into the Cavity of the Nostrils. In this Bone some say, there are also twelve Holes ; by the first and second ? ass the Optick Nerves ; by the rest pass other serves for the Motion of other Parts, as also of Veins and Arteries.

sphnopalatinus.c: SPHÆNOPALATINUS, is a Muscle of the Gargareon, which descends from a round fleshy Origination at a Process of the Os Sphanoidcs, which is in a direct Line between the Ala ZJefpertilionis, and Proccffus Styloides, thence it becomes a round fleshy Bely in half its Progress, grows less again near its latteral Insertion to the Posterior Part of the Gargareon. This with its Partner acting, draw the Gargareon with the ZJvula upwards and backwards ; which hinders the masticated Aliment from Regurgicating through the Foramina Narium in Deglutition.

sphnopharingus.c: SPHÆNOPHARINGÆUS, is a pair of Muscles arising from the Sinus of the inner Wing of the Os Cuneoforme, and going Obliquely downward, is extended into the Sides of the Gullet; it dilates the Gullet.

sphereofallivity.c: SPHERE of Allivity, of any Body, is that determinate Space or Extent all round about it, to which, and no farther, the Effluviums continually emitted from that Body do reach, and where they operate according to their Nature. Thus we see I the Magnetical Effluvia have certain Bounds and Limits, beyond which they will have no Influence to turn or to attract the Needle: But where-ever a Needle be placed, so as that it can be moved by a Load-stone, it may be laid to be within the Sfhere of Aflivity of the Stone.

spinallscotli.c: SPIN ALLS Cotli, is a Muscle so called, because it accompanies the Spines of the Neck ; it arises from the five Superior Transverse Processes of rhe Vertebra of the Thorax, and Inferior of the Neck, and in its Ascent becomes more fleshy, and is so inserted largely into the Inferior Part of the Vertebra of the Neck laterally, &c. These draw the Vertebra of the Neck directly backwards.

SPINSTER, a term in Law, being an addition usually given to all unmarried Women, from the Viscount’s Daughter downward. SPIRAL-U'we, in Geometry, is according to Archimedes thus generated. If a right Line as A B, having one end six’d at B, be equally moved round, so as with the other end B, to describe the Periphery of a Circle ; and at 1 the same time a Point be conceived to move forward equally from B towards A in the right Line B A, so as that the Point describes that Line, while the lane generates the Circle. Then will the Point with its two Motions describe-the curve Line B, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, Csc. C JA,,. 7 , 41 A which is called an Helix or Spiral Line ; and the plane Space contained between this Spiral Line and the Right Line B st, is called the Spiral Space. If also you conceive the Point B to move twice as flow as the Line A B, so as that it shall get but half way along B A when that Line shall have for6 Q med

S P 1 S P I mcd the Circle ; and if then you imagine a new Revolution to be made of the Line carrying the Point, so that they shall end their Motion at last together; there will be formed a Double Spiral Line, and two Spiral Spaces as you fee in the Figure; From the Genesis of which may easily be drawn these Corollaries. 1 . That the Lines Bn, B n, B 10, 5 $o; making equal Angles with the first and second Spiral, (as also B 12, B i o, B 8, ( 3 c,) are in Arithmetical Proportion. ' 2. The Lines B 7, B i o, ( 3 c. drawn any how to the first Spiral, arc to one another as the Arks of the Circle intercepted betwixt B A and those Lines. Because whatever parts of the Circumference the Point A describes, as suppose 7, the Point B will also have run over 7 Parts of the Line A B. 3. Any Lines drawn from B to the second Spiral, as B 18, B 22, (3 c. are to each other, as the aforesaid Arks, together with the whole Periphery added on both sides: For at the same time that the Point A runs over 12, or the whole Periphery, and perhaps 7 'parts more, shall that Point B have run over 12 and 7 parts of the Line A B, which is now supposed to be divided into 24 equal parts. CBc = 1, D B d — 4, and ABn= 9; and so it will be always, if you make never so many biifections of the 3 first Divisions of the Circle. That is, the Lines drawn front B to the Spiral, will be as 1,2,3,4,5,6, ( 3 c. and the Sectors circumscribed, as 1, 4, 25, 36,' ( 3 c. always going on in the order of Squares' or in a duplicate Ratio. (Or,) ' If another Circle be drawn with a Radiqs double to the former, its Area will be (as the Square of its Diameter) 4 times as great as that of the former. 1 therefore the first Circle to the second will be as 1 to 4, or as 3 to 12. And since the Spiral Space is to the first Circle as 1 to 3, that Space r 0 the second Circle will be as 1 to 12 ; and to a 3d Circle so described, as 1 to 27 ; to a 4th, as 1 to 48, ( 3 c. II. The first Spiral Line is equal to half the Peri' fhery of the first Circle ; for the Ifulii of the Sectors, and consequently the Arches are in simple Arithmetics Progression, while the Periphery of the Circle contains as many Arches equal to the greatest ; wherefore the Periphery to all those_ Arches,is to the Spiral-line as 2 to 1 (by N. 6 . of Arithm. Progrestion.) I thought one Proposition, with a Corollary or two, enough on this Subject, to give the Reader a Specimen of the Genesis, Nature and Properties, and way of Demonstration used about Spiral Lines: Those that would see more, m ay consult Archimedes, Dr. tVa/hs' s Arithmetics of Infinites, or Stutmius’ s Math. SPIRIT, which the Chymists call Merc u b > is one of the 5 Principles separable from a M. 1 ' by Fire ; ’tis subtil, light, penetrating, and ac j » and hath its Particles in a very quick .*

S P I S P o V This is probably that which causes the Growth and Encrease of all Bodies; but where it abounds most, those Bodies do soonest corrupt, because of its rapid motion. This appears in Vegetable and Animal Bodies,which yield the greatest Quantity of Spirit; whereas most Minerals, as having but a small proportion of Spirit in them, arc almost incorruptible. This Principle is never drawn pure, any more than the others; and when it comes over involved inalittle Oil/tis called an Ardent Spirit,such as Spirit of Wine ; which therefore should rather be called an Exalted Oil; and when it hath in it a little volatile Salt dissolved, ’tis called a Volatile Spirit, as the Spirit of Hartthorn, Urine, &c. If it be impregnated with Acid Salts, its volatility is then check’d, and ’tis called an Acid or Fixt Spirit, as Spirit of Salt, Vitriol, Allum, &c. which truly are only an Acid Salt dissolved and put into Fusion by a strong Fire.

spiritofniter.c: SPIRIT of Niter is thus drawn : Mix one part of Salt-perer with three times as much Pottersearth dried ; put this Mixture into a large Earthen Retort, and let it in a close Revcrberatory Fire ; distil off the Phlegm with a small Fire in about 4 or 5 Hours, and when no more Drops will come, Lute on a very large Receiver, and encrease the Fire gradually to the ad degree, some more volatile Spirits will come out in white Clouds : Keep the Fire thus about two Hours, and then encrease it to the greatest violence you can give it, the Vapours will come Red ; continue the Fire till no more red Fumes come; in 14 Hours the Operation will be over. If you used z Pounds of Nitre, you will draw 1 Pound 14 Ounces of Phlegm and Spirit together. The Vessels had need be large, and 1 of the Retort left empty, else there will be danger of breaking all to pieces, the Spirits come forth with that violence. This Spirit is the best Aqua-Forth, and is chiefly }ffed for Solution of Metals. But when dulcified, R a good Medicine Inwardly in many cases.

spiritofsalt.c: SPIRIT cf Salt, is made by drying and powdering the Salt, and then mixing of it with thrice its weight of Potters-Earth powdred : A Paste is made of these two with a little Rain-water, and then the Paste is made into little Balls or Pellets about as big as Nuts. A large Earthen Retort or Glass one coated, hath one third of it filled with these, and being placed in a Revcrberatory Fire, hath a large Receiver fitted to it. The Junctures must not "be Luted at first, but a very moderate Fire used for a time, to distil out all the Water : Rit as soon as yon see some little white Clouds a Ppear, throw out the insipid Liquor in the Receiver, and Lute it well to the Retort: Then encrease the Fire by degrees to the highest, and so mt it continue 1 a or 15 Hours, or till no more Clouds appear; when the Operation is ended, you "fill find the Spirit of Salt in the Receiver. Some, met isle this Spirit afterwards in a Cucurbite, by drawing off some of the weaker Spirit in a gentle hand-heat, and then what remains is very strong °f a yellow colour, and very weighty. Xt ^ equal parts of this acid Spirit and Spirit of ™mc are mixed together, and digested for about 1 °r 4 Days,- ’tis called Spirit of Salt duse sod. spirit of Salt will dissolve Leaf Gold, and will Precipitate what Aqua Forth hath dissolved. Which mews how very differently formed and figured the points and Pores of Acid Menstruum! may be, and ^sequent ly are.

spiritofsulphur.c: SPIRIT of Sulphur, commonly call’d Oil of Sulphur, by C ampanam,from the Vessels form being like a Glais Bell, in which it is usually Drawn) is only the acid Part of Sulphur turned into a Liquor by the means of Fire. Lemery uses a great Glass 1 unncl for this Operation • which seems to be the best way of drawing this Spirit, vid. p. 445, last FJitioti. __ Some make use of Salr-peter in the drawing of Spirit of Sulphur, but that is not a good Practice, because the Nitre alters something of the mixture of the Spirit.

spiritsinananimalbody.c: SPIRITS in an Animal Body, were reckon’d of three sorts; the Animal Spirits in the Brain, the Vital in the Heart, the Natural in the Liver: Bur late Authors distinguish ’cm only into two kinds ; the Animal in the Brain, the Vital and Natural (which are accounted the same) in the mass of Blood. The Animal Spirits arc a very thin Liquor, which distilling from the Blood in the outward or Cortical Substance of the Brain, are by the proper Ferment of the Brain exalted into Spirit, and thence through the Medullar Substance of the Brain, the Corpus Catlosum, and Medulla Ohlongata, are derived into the Nerves and Spinal Marrow, and in them perform all the Actions of Sense and Motion. The Vital or Natural Spirits are the subtilest parts of the Blood which actuate and ferment it, and make it fit for Nourishment.

splanchnica.c: SPLANCHNICA, are Medicines proper against Diseas es of the Intestines.

splen.c: SPLEN, five Lien, the Spleen, is a Receptacle for the salt and earthy Excrements of the Blood, that there, by the assistance of the Animal Spirits, it may be volatilized, and returning again into the Blood, may concur to its farther Fermentation. The Spleen consists of a great number of little Bladders, between which the Glandules are scattered up and down, and supply the place of Veins. The Spleen has likewise an Artery, Nerves, and Lymphatick Vessels, first discovert! by Fr. stiiiscb , says Blanchard. But you will find a much better Account of it in Gibson’s Anatomy, p. 106.

splenia.c: SPLENIA, are Bolsters made of Linnen, three, four, or five times doubled, even to the thickness of the Spleen : They are used upon Wounds, Ulcers, and Fractures. The Figure is threefold, according to the manner of Application, vi\. at length, obliquely, or tranfverfly : They are called also Plumaceoli, and Plagula. Blanchard.

spleniatickartery.c: SPLENIATICK Artery, is said by some to be the greatest branch of the Cceliaca , whence it goes to the Spleen, and therein ends.

splfniimusculi.c: SPLF.NII Musculi, arise partly from the five lower Vertebra: of the Neck ; and partly from the points of five of the upper Vertebra of the Thorax : The Fibres of these Muscles tend obliquely, and are fastened to the hinder part of the Head. The use of ’cm is to draw the Head backward. It hath its Name from its Figure, being something like to an Ox’s Spleen.

splice.c: SPLICE : at Sea they say a Cable or Rope is spliced, when the ends of two pieces being untwisted, the several Strands arc wrought into one another by a Fidd. Also when an Eye is to be made at the end of a Rope, the ends of the Strands are by a Fidd drawn into the ends of the other Ropes Strands, and this is called a Splice.

split.c: SPLIT ; the Seamen lay when a Sail is blown to pieces, it’s Split.

spoliation.c:

spondus.c: SPONDÆUS, is the Foot of a Latin Verse, consisting of two Syllables, and both of ’cm long, as Ingots.

spooning.c: SPOONING, when a Ship being under Sail in a Storm at Sea, cannot bear it, but is forced to put right before the Wind ; then the Seamen say, she Spoons ; and when in such a cafe there is danger lest lite should bring her Masts by the Board with her rowling about, or Seel under Water, and so Founder, they usually let up the Fore-sail to make her go the steadier, especially if there beSea-room enough ; and this they call Spooning with the Foresail.

spor.c: SPOR.ADIcI Morbi, arc those Diseases which (tho’ different in nature) seize several people at the lame time, and in the lame Country.

spotsinthesun.c:
SPOTS in the Sun. ’Tis certain those opake Masses which sometimes appear at the Sun, arc not Planets revolving at any,even the least distance from him, but Spots or MacuLc adhering to him ; for whereas they revolve but once in about 26 Days; on calculation it will appear, that a Planet near the Sun’s Surface, as these must be, cannot have above 3 Hours allowed for its periodical Revolution,which being so different from the fore mention’d space of 26 Days, quite decides that Controverlic, and demonstrates those Masses to be real Maculæ adhering to the Body of the Sun, as is here asserted. Anno 1660, April 27th, 8 H. A M. the Honourable Mr. Boyle observed a Spot in the lower Limb of the Sun, a little towards the South of its Equator, which was entred about st 0 of the Sun’s Diameter, it self being about ry-7 in itS shortest Diameter of that of the Sun, its longest about m, of the lame. May the 8th, about 1 o in the Morning, it appeared near about the same distance from the Westward Limb, a little South of its Equator ; tho’ at first it appear’d to be from the Eastward Limb, a little South also of its Equator. May the 9th, it disappeared. This Spot was very dark, and almost of a Quadrangular form, and was enclosed round with a kind of duskish Cloud. May the 2;th, the same Spot appear’d again, and seemed to be in a part of the same Line it had formerly traced,and was entered about st, ofitsDiameter, about 7 h. P. M. At which time, there appear’d another Spot, which upon its entrance was not above T ; T part of the Sun’s Diameter : It appear’d to be longest towards the North and South, and Ihortest towards the East and West; and there seemed to be dispersed about it divers small Clouds here and there. Anno 1671, August the nth, 6 h. P.M. Mr. Castini, by the help of a Three-foot Glass, observed in the Sun’s Disk two Spots very dark, and distant from his apparent Center about -j of his Sernidiameter. But, that he might the more exactly note their situation, in respect of the several Parts of the World, he made use of two very fine Th reds, cutting one another at Right Angles in the common Focus of the two Glasses, and in the Axis of the Telescope ; so that he might fee the Sun’s Center, and according as one of these Threds advance’d Westward, it marked in the Sun a Circle parallel to the Equator ; and the other Thred marked the Circle of Declination, or the Horary Circle. Then he observed that the Spots were in the Southern part of the Sun ; that their Elongation from this Parallel, passing through his Center, could be no more than about ~ r of his Diamctcrjand that they were situated on the Eastern-side in respect of the said Center of the Sun. He also Measured several times,from 6 a Clock at Night.to 7,the time which stapled between the passage of the Sun’s Center, and that of the first of these Spots, through the said Horary Circle, which sometimes he found to be 23, sometimes 22 Seconds, the Semidiametcr of the Sun then palling in 66 Seconds. August the 12th, he observed them from the time of st un-rifing, and perceived that now they were nearer his Center. The time between the pallage of the Sun’s Center, and that of the interior Edge of the Coronet which encompassed them both, was then of 16 Seconds. At 7 a Clock it was but of 15, and the Southern Limb of the Coronet touched the Parallel passing through the Sun’s Center. From 6 at Night unto 7, the time between the passage of the Sun’s Center and that of the Coronet’s Limb, was found to be one time of 8 Seconds, at another time of 7", and another of 7'' p. The distance of the Spots unto the Parallel, passing through the Sun’s Center, was near the same on the North-iidc, with what it hath been observed to be in the Morning on the South-side. August the 13th, about 6 in the Morning, the edge of the Coroner was distant from the Equator, on the North-side, 30 Seconds; and there was but one Second of Time from the passage of the Sun’s Center into the passage of the lame anterior Edge of the Coronet. At 8 h. 30', the Fore-edge was in the same Horary Circle with the Sun’s Center ; so that in one Day and an half, these Spots have run through very near the third part of the Sun’s apparent Scmidiameter, which giveth an Arch of 19 Dcgr. 30 Min. of the circumference of the Sun’s Body ; and consequently, their Diurnal Motion about the Sun’s Axis hath been of 13 Deg. and the time of their periodical Revolution, as far as could be conjectured in so little Time, must be about 27 Days and an half; which was confirmed afterwards by farther Observations. Phil. Trans. Aug. the 30th, 1671, Dr. Hoolp observed a large Spot in the Center of the Sun’s Face .about Noon. Sept. the 1 st, he saw the same Spot again, and observed it to be moved about st of the Sun’s Diameter Westward. April the 25th 1683, Mr. Flamstcad sim a large Spot, having 3' 40" more North Declination than the Sun’s Center, and at 3 li. 3 5 1 after Noon he measured its Distance from the next o', 40". . April the 26th, hc saw it more remote from the Limb, and at 8 a clock determined its Longitude from the Sun’s Axis 66 st Dcgr. and its Declination from the Solar Equator 8 st Deg. South. . The Revolution of this Spot, Mr. Flatnsten ^ found to confirm his former 1 heQry of the Sun s Motion round his Axis in 25 d. 6 It. and that t e Angle of his Equator and our Ecliptick is 7 Dstgand the Longitude of his Northern Pole was m W 16°. springoftheair.c: SPRING of the Air, or its Elastical Force, fee wore in Air. That there is such a Spring or Elasticity in the Air, is clear from the following Experiments. i. That Bladders but half blown up, and having their Necks well tied, did swell in the exhausted Receiver as if blown to their full Dimensions ; and that full blown Bladders, and even thin square Glass Viols well stop’d, will break to pieces when' once the Air is well pump’d out of the Receiver. i. A glass Syphon, whose recurved Leg was turn’d up parallel to the upper and longer, and was scaled Hermetically at the end of the lesser or shorter Leg, had a quantity of Quicksilver poured into it, and by its being moved often up and down, the Air in the sealed and shorter Leg, was brought to the same Temperament of the External. After this, more Mercury was poured in, till the Air in the sealed Leg was compressed into about half its usual Dimensions, and then the Mercury in the longer Leg was 29 Inches higher than that in the shorter: By which it appears plainly, That the Spring of the Air in the sealed Leg was so great, as to equiponderate a Column of Mercury of 29 Inches in Length. Boyle against Sinus. 3. A Viol silled to but a 4th part with Quicksilver, had a long and slender glass Pipe fastened into its Neck, with Sealing-Wax or Cement,whose lower Orifice was a good way under the Quicksilver in the Viol; then having blown in a little Air, to try whether the Viol were well stop’d, it Was conveyed into a long and slender Receiver ; and after the Air was drawn off by the Pump, the Spring of the included Air within the Bottle, impelled the Mercury up to the Height of 27 Inches in the pipe,and there kept it suspended still upon the read mission of the Air,the Quicksilver fell down to its first station in the Pipe. This Experiment Mr. B.ylc often tried, and with desired : ucccfs. And when it was tried with a Bottle that held a Quart, the Spring of such a Quantity of Air was able to raise the Mercury up to 29 Inches f. But nothing could make it raise above the common Height of the Quicksilver in the Baroscope. 4. Into a C opper Vessel of a Cylindrical shape, Was put almost Water enough to sill it, and then was immersed into it and kept under Water by a height, a square glass Viol that would hold 9 or 1 o Ounces of Water, and was well stop’d : After this, Mr. Boyle placed the Copper Vessel in bis Pneumatical Engine, and pumping up the Air, be found, That the Spring of the Air included in die Viol broke it all to pieces, tho’under Water, with a great Noise, and made a kind of Smoak or Mist" appear above the Surface of the Water. Which Experiment proves both the great Force of the Natural Spring of the Air, when the weight of the Atmosphere is removed ; and also that the Weight of the Atmosphere acts upon Bodies under V’ater; for that could by its universal pressure beep the Spring-of the Air in the Bottle bent while it was under the Surface of the Water; but when once that, by plying the Tump, was taken off, the Elastick Particles unbent themselves violently, and broke the Viol. See the Experiments about the Pressure of the Airs Spring on Bodies under Water. The Spiing of the Air, is equal every where in a Natural state to the weight of the IncumbentAtmoIpherc • just as if a Person should squeeze or compress together either by the force of his Hand, or bY a Weight, any parcel of Wool, or such Elastick Bodies,the Wool would by its Spring equally press against the Hand or Weight. According to the zd Axiom of Mr. Newton’s Principia, Atlionicon-. tr arian semper & equal em esse Rgailioncm. The Accurate Dr. Hool<_ on Experiments well made, thinks we may conclude the Spring of the Air to be Reciprocal to its Extension. Micrograph. p. 227. And the Resistance of the Spring of the Air, is found to be nearly equal to the Weight or Force that compresses it; and the Spaces that the same Air occupies under differing Pressures, arc Reciprocally as those Pressures. The Quantity of the dilatation and expansion of Air only by the Operation of its Spring, without any additional Heat, Mr. Boyle found to be so great, that a Bubble of Air included in a proper Glass Pipe almost filled with Water, was extended to above 150 times its former Dimensions; and he believes would have taken up 200 times its former room, had the Tube been long enough to have tried the Experiment. New. Expcr. Phjs. Mech. Edit. i.p. 32,33. He found also, that a Cylinder of Air of an Inch in Diameter, and less than two Inches in Length, would, when included in a Bladder, and the weight of the Atmosphere taken off by Pumping, by its bare Spring only, raise a weight of above 1 o Pounds Averdupois. He found also, that the Spring of a Cylinder of Air of 2 Inches Diameter, and of the former length, was in the same Engine able to raise up 42 Pound weight. Whence it appears, that the Force of the Spring of different Cylinders of Air is in a duplicate Ratio, to the Diameters of those Cylinders. The Spring of the Air, may be explicated either by supposing the Air near the Earth to consist of an Heap of such little Springy or Elastick Bodies lying one upon another resembling those of a Fleece of Wool: Or else, according to D. Cartes his way, by supposing, That the Air is nothing but a Congeries of flexible Particles of several kinds of Figures and Sizes, which are raised by Heat into the fluid and subtil Ethereal Matter that surrounds the Earth, and by the continual agitation of that Matter , wherein those Particles swim, arc so whirled about, that each Corpuscle endeavours to beat off all others from coming within the little Sphere requisite to its Motion about its own Center, and fin cafe any, by intruding into that Sphere shall oppose its free Rotation) to drive it away.

springamast.c:
SPRING a Mast ; so the Seamen call it, when a Mast is only crack’d, but not quite broken, in any part of her; as in the Partners, the Hounds, &c.. then they say, The Mast is Sprung. SPRING-^rAer, in a Watch, is that part in the middle of the Spring Box which the Spring is wound or turned about, and to which it is hooked at one end. SPRING-Bor, is that Cylindrical Case or Frame that contains within it the Spring of a Watch or other Movement. SPRING-Tn/c, is the increasing higher of a Tide after a dead Neipc; this is about 3 Days before the Full or Change of the Moon ; but the top or highest of the Spring-Tide is 3 Days after the Full or Change; then the Water runs highest with the Flood, andjowest with the Ebb, and the Tides run more strong and swift than in die Neipes. springsandfountains.c:
SPRINGS and Fountains. Concerning the Origin of these, there is much Dispute, especially of fetch as are found on the tops of high Mountains. Some, as Dr. Hook., Dr. Plotr, and many others, think that they arise from the Sea-water percolated through the Bowels of the Earth, which by that means being deprived of its Salt, is rend red much Lighter than before, and so is capable of Riling up to the height we commonly find Springs at, as Water Riles in a Filtre, or in very small Tubes, 6c. And Dr. Hook, hath a pretty Experiment about this, in his Microgr.p. a;. But I cannot see how by this Hypothesis, fuposingthe Gravity of the whole Atmoiphcrc could c taken off, Water can rise above 34 or 35 Foot above the level of the Ocean. The Learned Capt. Halley supposes them to be caused from the Vapours exhaled by the Sun out of the Sea, 6 c. Of which, sec an Account under the Word Vapour 1 The Ingenious Dr. Woodward, in his Natural History of the Earth supposes, That the great Abyss of Waters, placed in the Bowels of the Earth, is the standing Fund and Promptuary which supplies Water to the Surface of the Earth, and furnishes as well Springs and Rivers, as Vapours and Rain. For he asserts, That there is a nearly uniform, and constant Fire or Heat, disseminated thro’our the Body of the Earth, and especially in the Inferior parts of it: The Bottoms of the deeper Mines Being very sultry, and the .Stone and Ores there being very sensibly hot even in Winter. That 'tis this Subterraneous Heat which evaporates and elevates the Waters of the Abyss, buoying it up indifferently on all Sides, and towards all parts of the Surface of the Globe. That this rising Vapour, or Water, pervades not only the Fissures and Intervals of the Stone,but,the very Bodies of the Strata them selves,permeating the Interstices of the Sand,Earth,or other matter,whereof they consist ; yea, even the most firm and dense Marble and Sand-Stone; for these give admission to it, tho’ in lesser Quantity, and are always found saturated with it; which is the reason that they are softer, and can be cut much more easily when they arc first taken out of the Earth, than they can afterwards, when they have lain some time exposed to the Air, and when that Humidity is evaporated. This Vapour he asserts to proceed directly up towards the Surface of the Globe, on all sides, unless when impeded and diverted by the Interposition of Strata of Marble, the denser sorts of Stone, or either like Matter, which is so close and compact, that it can admit it Only in a smaller Quantity, aud this very slowly too. And when it is thus intercepted in its Passage, the Vapour, which cannot penetrate the Stratum directly, will some of it glide along the lower Surface of the Stratum, permeating the Horizontal Interval, which is betwixt that and the next Stratum lying underneath it; the rest will pass the Interstices of the Mais of the subjacent Strata, whether they be of laxer Stone, of Sand, Marie, or the like, with a Direction parallel to the site of those Strata, till it arrives at their perpendicular Intervals. And when the Water is once come to these Intervals, in case the Strata, whereby the ascending Vapour wa,s collected and condensed into Water, fas we usually speak) in like manner as by an Alcmbick, happen to be raised above the Level ot the Earths Surface ; as those Strata always are,whereof Mountains do consist ; then the Water, being likewise got above the said Level, flows forth ot those Intervals or Apertures; and if there be no Obstacle without, forms Brooks and stivers. Bur where the Strata, which so condense it, are not higher than the mean Surface of the Earth, it stag' nates at the Apertures, and only forms standing Springs. He adds, That tho' this Supply of Water from the Abyss, be continual, and nearly the same at all Seasons, and alike to all parts of the Globe, y cc when it arrives at or near the Surface of the Earth, where the Heat (the Agent which evaporates and bears it up) is not so constant and uniform, as is that resident within the Globe,but is subject to Vicissitudes and Alterations, being at certain Seasons greater than at others; being also greater in some Climates and Parts of the Earth than in others: R thence happens that the Quantity of Water at the Surface of the Earth, tho' sent up from the Abyss with an almost constant equality, is various and uncertain, as is the Heat there ax some Seasons, and in some Countries, the Surface abounding, and being even drown’d with the Plenty of it, the Springs full, and the Rivers high : At other Seasons, and in other Countries, both Springs and Rivers may be exceeding low, and sometimes totally fail. When the Heat in the exterior parts of the Earth, and in the Ambient Air, is as intense as that in the interior parts of it, then all that Water which passes the Strata directly, mounting up in separate Parcels, or in Form of Vapour, does not stop at the Surface, because the Heat there, is equal both in Quantity aud Power to That underneath, which brought it out of the Abyss. This Heat therefore takes it here, and hears it up> part of it immediately out at the Surface of the Earth; the rest thro’the Tubes and Vessels of the Vegetables which grow thereon, Herbs, Shrubs, and Trees, and along with it a sort of Vegetative Terrestrial Matter, which it detaches from out the uppermost Stratum wherein these are placed ; this it deposes in them for their Nutriment, as it passes thro’ 'em, and issuing out at their Tops and Extremities, it marches still on, and is elevated up into the Atmosphere, to such an height, that the Heat there being less, it becomes condensed, unites and .combines into small Masses, or Drops, and at length falls down again in stain, Dew, Hail, ° r Snow. And for the other part of the Water which was condensed at the Surface of the Earth, and sent forth collectively into standing Springs and stivers ; { h K also sustains a Diminution from the Heat above, being evaporated more or less in properties to the greater or lesser Intenseness of the Heat, and the greater or lesser Extent of the Surface of the Water to sent forth. And as these Evaporations arc at sometimes greater, according to the greater Heat of the Sun, so where ever they alight again in Rain, 'tis so n\ uC superior in Quantity to the Rain of colder Season*? as the Sun’s Power is then superior to its Power m Those Seasons : This is apparent in our Northern Clime, where the Sun’s Power is never very great, but yet our Rains in June, sidy, and August ‘"V much greater than those of the colder Months, 1 ^ Drops larger, and consequently heavier, falling much thicker and faster than at ot times. t,.,-

S Q U SQU But much more apparent is this in the Regions ot the Earth, nearer to, or under the Equator, where the Sun having a much greater force, their Rains (which arc Periodical, happening usually about the same time, and lasting several Months) fall in such Quantities as to be more like descending Rivers than Showers; and by these are caused the mighty Inundations of the Nile, and other Rimers in thole Regions. But when the Heat in the exterior parts of the Earth, and in the Ambient Air, is less than that in the Interior ; the Evaporations are likewise less; and the Springs and Rivers do not only cease to be diminished, proportionably to the Relaxation of the Heat, but are much augmented, a great part ot the Water which ascends to the Surface of the Earth, stopping there for want of Heat to mount it thence «p into the Atmosphere, and saturating the superficial, or uppermost Strata with Water; which by degree? drains down into Wells, Springs, and Rivers, and so makes an Addition to them ; and is the Reason that these abound with Water in the Colder Seasons, so much more than they do in the Hotter. And the Water which is thus dispensed to the Earth and Atmosphere from the great Abyss, being carried down by Rains and by RJvcrs, into the Ocean, which communicates with the Abyss, is by that means restored back again to it; and from thence it returns again in a continual Circulation, to the Surface of the Earth, in Vapours and Springs.

springy.c: SPRINGY, or Elastics Bodies, arc such, as having h a j t h c i r Figure changed by the Stroak or Bercuifion of another Body, can recover again their former Figure; which Bodies which arc not Elastical will not do. Thus, If a piece of Steel he bent any way, it will recover again its former straitness, but a piece of Lead will stand bent in any form.

spungingofagreatgun.c: SPUNGING of a great Gun, is clearing of her Inside, after Ihe hath been discharged, with a Wad of Sheep-skins, or the like, rolled about one end of the Rammer: Its design is to prevent any parts of Fire from remaining in her; which would endanger the Life of him who should load, or charge her again.

spunyarn.c: SPUN-YARN, is Rope-yarn, whose Ends arc beaten, or scraped thin, in order to fasten one piece to another, that so it may be as long as is necessary: It is of use to make Caburns, and for uiany other Purposes aboard a Ship.

spurkets.c: SPURKETS, are the Spaces in a Ships Side, betwixt the upper and lower Futtocks, or betwixt the Rungs fore and aft.

squammosasutura.c: SQUAMMOSA Sutura, is one of the Sutures of *hc Bones of the Skull ; so called, because the 1 arts of the Bones united by the Suture, do lie ver V Hope, and like Scales.
