squaring.c: SQUARING. By the Word Squaring, Mathematicians understand the making ot a Square equal to any Figure given. Thus the Quadrature or Squaring of the Circle, is the finding a Square equal to the Area of a Circle, which hath not yet been done Geometrically.

squinancy.c: SQUINANCY, or Quinsy, a Swelling and Inflammation in the Throat. See Angina*, Sl'AGMA, arc Juices of Plants mrx’d together in order to Distillation.

stalactit.c: STALACTITÆ, arc a sort of stony, sparry Iceycles which hang down from the Tops or Arches of Grotto’s, Caves, or Subterranean Caverns, and from the Roofs of the Buildings and Capitals of the Pillars of such Places as ave built over the Thermic or Hot Springs. Ot this kind are the Sal Alumen and Vitriolum Stalailitum, the Mincra Ferri-ftalatlica, the Vitriolum Capillare , and the AlumenCapillare, 8c c. These Stalacticce Dr. As de</- ward faith, should rather be called Stagonit.e.

stamina.c: STAMINA, in Botany, are thole littler fine Thrcds or Capil-laments which grow up within the Flowers of Plants encompassing round the Style, and on which the Apices grow, at their extremities. Whence the Botanists call that a

stamintousflower.c: STAMINTOUS Flower, which is so far imperfect, as to want those coloured Leaves which are Galled Pet alæ, and consists only of the Stylus and the Stamina. And such Plants as do bear these Staminceus Flowers Mr. Ray, makes to constitute a large Genus of Plants, which he calls Herbx store Imperfecto five ape tale Stamineove. And these he divides into such as, 1. Have their Fruit or Seed totally divided from the Flower ; and these are such Plants as are said to be of different Sexes : The reason of which is, that from the same Seed some Plants shall arise with Flowers and no Fruit, and others with Fruit and no Flowers : As Hops, Hemp, stinging Nettles, Spinach, Cynocramhe, Mercurials, and Phyllon. 2. Such as have their Fruit only a little disjoin’d from their Flowers ; as the Ambrosia, Bardana minor, Ricinus, and the Helitropium Tricoccon. z. Such as have their Fruit immediately contiguous, or adhering to their Flower : And the Seed of these is either, 1. Triangular .- And of this sort, some arc lucid and sliining, as the Lapathum, Rliaborbarum, and Bisiorta ; to which also may be reckoned the Peisiceria. Others arc rough and not sinning; as the Helleborus Albus, Fegopyrum, Convolvulus niger, and I he Polygonum. 2. Such as have a roundish Seed a little flatted or compressed, or of any other Figure but the former Triquetrous or Triangular one. And these have their Flower, or the Calyx of the Flower adhering to the Bottom or Basis of the Seed or Fruit; as the Potamogiton, Blitum Silvistre, Parietaria, Atriplex, Blitum Sativum, Amuranthcs Holocerkeus, and the Saxifraga Aurea. z. Such whose Flowers adhere to the top or uppermost of the Seed; as the Beta, Afarttm, Alchimilla, S T A And to these kind of Plants, Mr. Ray reduces also the Kaligeniculatum, Sedum fruticofum, the Secparia, or Bctviderc of the Italians.

stanchionsinaship.c: STANCHIONS in a Ship, arc thole limbers which being let up Pillarwilc, do support and strengthen the wast Trees.

standingpartofthesheat.c: STANDING Part of the Sheat, is that part which is made fast to a Ring at the Ship’s Quarter. When they say, Over-hale the Sheat, they mean, Hale upon the standing Part ; But when they say, Hale the Sheat barely, they intend it only ol the Running Part. S 1 And ing Rppcs, are those Ropes which d° not run in any Blocks, but arc set taught, or let (lack, as occasion serves, as the Sheat-stays, Backstays, and the like. SI AND 1 NG Part of a Tackle aboard a Ship* is the end of the Rope where the Block is seized or fastned ; as the other which is haled, is called Fa/h

stapes.c: STAPES, or the Stirrop, because of its resemblance to a Stirrop, is a little Bone in the Ear, ot a Triangular Figure, and is made of two Branches set upon a flat Basis, which stands upon the Foramen Ovate ; the uniop of the two Branches is called the Head of the Stapes, in which there is a small Cavity, ypherein lies another little Bone.

staphyloma.c: STAPHYLOMA, is a Disease of the Eye, ir> which the two Tunicks of the Eye, Cornea aud Vvea, being broken, fall outward in the shape ot a Grape.

star.c: STAR, in Fortification, is a Work with several Faces, generally composed of from 5 to 8 Points, with saliant, and Rc-entring Angles Flanking one another; every one of its Sides containing from 12 to Fathoms.

starboard.c: STARBOARD, the Right-hand side of a Ship* as Larboard is the left .- Thus they say, Starboard the Helm, or Helm a ' tar board; when he that Conds would have the Man at the Helm put the Helm to the Right-side of the Ship. STAR-i-Vr. See Fort.

staticalbaroscope.c: STATICAL Baroscope, an Instrument Invented by the Honourable Mr. R. Boyle, whose Description fee in Baroscope. SI ATICAL Hygrosoope. Sec Hygroscope.

staticks.c: STATICKS, is a Science purely Speculative, being a Species of Mechanickj, conversant about Weights, and shewing the Properties of the Floavincss and Lightness, or Equilibria of Bodies. When it is restrained to the Specifick Weights and Equilibria of Liquors, it is called Hydrostatics i which see.

station.c: STATION, in Astronomy, signifies certain Places of the sipdiach_, where a Planet being arrived, seems to stand still for some time in the same Degree, either in ascending to its Apogee, or descending to its Perigee.

STATION, is a Place where a Man fixes himself and his Instruments, to take (as in Surveying! any Angles or Distances. Station-L inc. See Line of Station. - STATION-SVq/f, is an Instrument consisting 0 two Rulers that slide to ten Foot, divided into Feet and Inches, with a moving Vane or ’ two of which are used with a Level; and ou m Edg*s, there are the Links of the Gunters Cham divided. It is used in Surveying for the moreea 1 takijig Off-scts. STAS T A S T E

stationaryiaplanet.c: STATIONARY i a Planet is Hud to be Stationery, when to any Eye placed on the Earth, it appears for some time to stand still, and to have no progressive Motion forward in its Orbit round the Sun.

statute.c: STATUTE, is a Word that hath divers significations : as first, it signifies an Atst of Parliament made by the King and the Three Estates of the Realm ; in which sense it is either General or Special. In another signification, Statute is a Short Writing, called a Statute-Mcrchant, or a Statute Staple ; which see. Statutes arc also vulgarly taken for the Fetit-Sestions, by ; Eli%. cap. 4. STATUTE-Mcrc/j/wr, is a Bond acknowledged before one of the Clerks of the SA<7fKs«-Merchant and Mayor, or Chief Warden of the City of London, or two Merchants ot the said City for that purpose assigned, or before the Mayor, Chief Warden, or Master of other Cities or good Towns, or other sufficient Men for that purpose appointed, Sealed with the Seal of the Debtor and of the King, which is of two pieces; the greater is kept by the Mayor, Chief-Warden, £se. and the lesser by the laid Clerks. STATUTE-5>4/)/e, is so called either Properly or Improperly. A Statutc-Staple, properly so called, is a Bond of Record, acknowledged before the Mayor of the Staple, in the Presence of one of tire two Constables ot the lame Staple ; for which Seal, the Fee is of every Pound, if the Sum exceed not 100 I. an Halfpenny ; and if it exceed loo /. a Farthing ; and by virtue of such Statute staple, the Creditor may forthwith have Execution of the Body, Lands, and Goods of the Debtor. Statutc-Staple improper, is a Bond of Record, founded upon the Stat. 23 H. 8. cap. 6. Of the nature of a proper Statute-Staple, as to the Force and Execution of it; and acknowledged before one ot the Chief Justices ; and in their Absence, before the Mayor of the Staple, and Recorder of London.

statutumdelaborariis.c: STATUTUM dc Laborariis, is a Writ Judicial, for the Apprehending of such Labourers as refuse to Work according to the Statute, l\eg. Judic. sol. 27.

statutomercatorio.c: STATUTO Mercntorio, is a Writ for the Imprisoning of him that has forfeited a Bond called Statutc-Mcrchant, until the Debt be satisfied. Of these, there is one against Lay-persons, and another a gainst Ecclesiastical. STATUTO5 >/!/issr, is a Writ that lies to take his Body to Prison, and seize upon his Lands and Goods, that hath forfeited a Bond called Statute staple. oTAYS in a Ship, arc Ropes whoso use is to keep the Mast from falling aft : All Masts, TopMasts.and Flag-Stavcs have Stays, except the Sprirfail Top-mast ; the Stay of the ‘Main-mast, which ri called the Main-stay, is by a Lannier fastned to a Golkar, which - comes about a Knee belonging to the Head ; the Main-top-mast Stay, is fastned to the Head of the Forc-mast, by a Strap and a dead Man’s Eye, and so is the Main-top-gallant-mast hayed to the Head of the Fore-top-mast ; the Eorc-niast and Masts belonging to it, are in the Jatne manner stayed to the Bolt-sprit and Spritsail Eop-sail Mast, which Stays do likewise stay the bolt sprit it self. The Mijsen-stay comes to the Main-mast by the Half-Dcck, and the Topmasthays come to the Shrouds with Crows-feet. The Efngth of the Stay is the same ' vith chat of the Mast it belongs to. The main-mast,Forc-mast,with them acts belonging to them, have also Backstays, which help to keep the Mast from pitching forward, or overboard, because they go on either side of the Ship ; To bring a Ship upon the

stayes.c: STAYES, or to Jlay her, is in order to her Tacking, which is thus done: At the same time bear up the Helm, let jly the Fore-fail Sheas, let go the Forebowling, Brace the Heat her-brace of the Fore-fail ; the same is also done to the Topsail and Top-gallant sail, only their Shears must be kept fast. If the Sprit-fa.il be out, then at the sometime let go the Sprit-fail Sheat also, with the Fore-sheet, and Brace the H^catcher-brace : But the Tacky, Sheats, Bracings , and Bowlings, of the Mainsail, Maiti-top-sail, and Mijscn are not altered. And when the Wind comes in at the Bow, which before was the Lec-Bow, it drives all the Sails backward against the Shrouds and Masts, so that the Ship makes no way forward, but drives with her Broad-side. Those are reckoned the best Ships, which will stay with the fewest Sails.

steady.c: STEADY, a Word of Command at Sea, from him that Conns to the Man at Helm, to keep the Ship steady in her Course, and not to make Angles or Yaws (as they call them) in or out.

steatocele.c: STEATOCELE, is a Rupture or Tumor in the Scrotum of a Fatty or Suet-like Consistence. Blanchard. STEATOfyIA,is a preternatural Swelling which consists of a Matter almost like Suet, of the same Colour throughout, soft; and tho’ not easily yielding to the Touch, yet suddenly returns, the Fingers being removed, to its proper Shape and Bigness.

steel.c: STEEL, is made, according to Mr. Lemery, p. 154, by Stratifying of Plates of Iron in a large Furnace, with the Horns or Nails of Animals, under which is made a very great Fire .- Thus is the Iron calcined ; but when red Hot, and near Melting, they take the Plates out and dip them suddenly in cold Water, and so they become Steel. Steel is not so good as Iron for Medicinal Opera - tion, because the volatile Parts are mostly purged away in the Calcination, and what remains is hardly dissolvable by the Juice in the Body.

steer.c: STEER : To Steer a Ship, is to guide or govern her by the Helm.He is the best Steersman that uses the least Motion in putting the Helm over to and again,and that keeps the Ship best from making Yaws ; that is, from running in and out. There arc three ways to Steer by. 1. By any Mark on the Land, so as to keep the Ship Even by it. 2. By the Compass, which is to keep the Ship’s Head upon such a Rumb or Point of the Compass, as best leads to her desired Port. 3. To Steer as one is bidden or Condcd, which is the Duty (in a great Ship)of him that is taking his Turn at Helm.

steerage.c:
STEERAGE, a Part of a Ship where he standeth that Steereth ; that is, Guides the Helm or Bytddcr of the Ship ; and this in a Man of War is always before the Bulk-head of the great Cabbin ; and where-ever the Steersman be placed, he must stand so, as that he can see the Leetch of the Sails, whether they be in the Wind or nor. <5 R z STEEVE

steeve.c: STEEVE j the Seamen say that the Bowsprit or the Beas-bead of the Ship doth Stecvc, when either stands too upright, and not strait enough forwards.

steganography.c: STEGANOGRAPHY, is the Art of secret Writing, which is known only to the Persons corresponding with one another; and which, it the Letters should be Opened, no one is supposed to be able to discover, or Decipher, as 'tis called. Tho now-a-days hardly any thing can be W ritten by this Art, but what may be Dccyphcrcd, and the Sense and Meaning of it discovered. And in this Art of Deciphering, that Excellent Mathematician Dr. iValin, is admirably ready.

stegnosis.c: STEGNOSIS, is a constriction or stopping upfof the Pores - STEGNQTICA. See Astringentia.

stellateblunts.c: STELLATE Blunts, arc by the Botanists called such Plants as have their Leaves growing on the Stalks at certain Intervals or Distances, in the form of a Radiant Star; and according to Mr. Ray, this is the Tenth Genus of English Plants : Of this kind is Cruciata or Cross-wort, Mollugo, iv lint adder, Afperula or Woodruff, Gallium or hadis Bed-straw, Aparine or Cleavers, Bjibia Tinclorum or Dyers Madder. To which he adds, as a-kin to this Genus, the Nasturtium Indicu >>, Indian Crefie, or Yellow Larkspur.

stemofaship.c: STEM of a Ship, is that main piece of Timber which comes bowing or bending from the Keel below, where it is scarfed, (as they call it) that is, pieced in, right before the Fore-castle ; this Stem it is which guides the Rake ot the Ship; and all the But-ends of the Planks (forwards) are six’d into it. This in the Section of a First-Rate Ship, is called the Main-stem. STENTORO-PHONICK-T«£e, or Instrument, is the Speaking-Trumpet, Invented by Sir Samuel Morcland.

step.c: STEP, that pcece of Timber in a Ship whereon the Masts or Capstans do stand at Bottom, is called the Step of the Mast or Capstan.

stercorosusfluxus.c: STERCOROSUS Fluxus, is that in which much Liquid Excrement is often voided, proceeding from Excrementitious Meats corrupted in the Stomach, or a great quantity of Excrements heaped up in the Intestines. Blanchard.

stereobata.c: STEREOBATA, in Architecture, is the Greeks Word for the first beginning of the Wall of any Building, and immediately standing on the Foundation : This is wrongly confounded with Stylobata, which is the beginning of a Column, or its Pedestal.

stereography.c: STEREOGRAPHY, is the Art of drawing the forms of .Solids upon a Plane. STEREOGRAPHICK Prose union. See Projeflion of the Sphere in Pleno.

stereometry.c: STEREOMETRY, is the Art of Mtafuring all forts of Solid Bodies; which how to do, you will find under the proper Names of each Body.

sternofaship.c: STERN of a Ship, is all the hindermost or aftermost Part of her, generally speaking : But properly, ’tis only the outmost Part of her, Abaft.

sternfast.c: STERNFAST, is some fastenings of Rqx’s, G?c. behind the Stern of a Ship, to which a Cable or Hawser may be brought or fixed, in order to hold her Stern to awharfe. £?c.

sternpost.c: STERNPOST, is a great Timber let into the Keel at the Stern of a Ship, somewhat sloping, into which arc fastned the after Planks; and on this Post, by its Pintle and Gudgeons hangs the Rudder.

sternohyoides.c: STERNOHYOIDES, is that Pair of Muscles # which is commonly by Anatomists said to arise front the uppermost part of the Breast-Bone : But this is since proved a Mistake, for they arise from the Internal part of the Clavieula, next where its Origination is broad and fleshy, and ascends directly over the Sternothyrcoideus and Larynx, ot an equal Breadth and Thickness, to its Insertion at the Basis of the Fore-Bone of the Os Hyoides. This with its Partner acting, pulls the Os Hyoides, together with the Tongue and Larynx, directly downwards.

sternothyroeidf.c: STERNOTHYROEIDF.S, is a pair of Muscles which do arise broad and fleshy from the upper and internal Part of the Sternum , whence ascending on the sides of the Wind-pipe, over the Glandule Tbyroideœ, it’s inserted to the in serious Part of the Thyroid al or Scutiformal Cartilage. This, with its Partner, pulls the Larynx downward, and lengthens the Canalis or distance between the Rimula and Tip of the Tongue, (which latter seems to be the true PleBrum Vocn) whereby the Tone of the Voice is rendered grave.

sternumof.c: STERNUM Of, the Breast-Bone, is joined to the Ribs in the foremost part of the Breast, consisting of 3 or 4 Bones, and frequently in those that arc come to ripeness of Age, grows into one Bone ; to this is joined in the lower part of it, the Cartilage Lasts or mis.

sternutation.c: STERNUTATION, Sneezing, is a forcible driving out of the Head some sharp Matter which vellicates and disturbs the Nerves and Fibres ■ Or, as some say, ’tis an involuntary Motion of the Brain, which contracts the Muscles of the Thorax and Abdomen, to the intent that the Matter which vellicates the Nostrils and Brain may be driven out.

sternutatorium.c: STERNUTATORIUM, five Sternutamentum, a Sneezing Medicine, or Snuff.

stewardofaship.c: STEWARD of a Ship, is he that receives all the Victuals from the Purser; and he is to see R well Stowed in the Hold ; in his Custody are all things of that nature belonging to the Ship’s useHe is ro look after the Bread, and to distribute out the several Messes of Victuals in the Ship. He hath an Apartment for himself in the Hold, which is called the Steward’s Room, where he Sleeps and Eats.

stile.c: STILE, in Dyalling, is the Gnomon or Cock of a Dyal, that casts the Shadow upon the Hour lines; and is always parallel to the Axis of the Earth, in all kinds of Dyals.

stillatitiousoils.c: STILLATITIOUS Oils, in Chymistry, are such as arc Extracted out of Mixts, by the Force of Fire ; and hereby are distinguished from fn cti as are made by Expression, or by Pressing. STILLICIDIUM ZJrin.c. Sec Stranrurid.

stirrupofaship.c: STIRRUP of a Ship, is a pecce of Timber put on upon a Ship’s Keel, when some of her K ee happens to be beaten off, and they can’t come convent ly to put or fit in a new piece ; then they patch in a piece of Timber, and bind it on wit an Iron which goes under the Ship’s Keel and come* up on each Side of the Ship, where 'tis Naiq strongly with Spikes ; and this they call a St if' TUp. i

stoaked.c:
STOAKED, when in a Ship the Water in t«e Bottom can’t come to the Well of the Pump, th f say, The Ship is a-stoak_, or stoaked : So they * also, The Limber-holes arc stoaked, when the cannot pass through them ; and that the P ul ^f , s stoaked, when something is got into it which c it up, so that it will not Work. stocks.c: STOCKS ; so the Ship-Carpenrers call a Frame of Timber, aud great Posts made a-sliore to build Pinnaces, Ketches, Boats, and such small Craft, and sometimes small Frigats : Hence we say, a Ship is on the Stocks, when (he is a Building.

stolones.c: STOLONES, arc the Suckers which spring up from the hoot of any Tree or Plant; and which, if nor cut off, will hinder the Thriving of the Tree,

stomachus.c: STOM ACHUS, in Anatomy,is nor the Stomach of an Animal, tor chat is called Ventriculus ; but is properly the left or upper Orifice of the Ventricle, or Stomach, by which Meats are received into it. To this Part descend Nerves from the eighth Pair and intercostal Nerves, and are mixed and interwoven with one another. The Gref/y call it -c-ori's, the Heart Whence it is that a Pain which is sometimes felt in this Part, is corruptly called the Heartburn ; and the Region of the stomach here about is called also S crobiculus Cor dis, or the Heart-Pit. stopper.c: STOPPER, is a piece of Rope (in a Ship) having a Wale-knot at one end, with a Larmier spliced into it, and at the other end ’tis made fast in the Place where ’tis to be tiled. Its use is to stop the main Halliards, or the Cable. The Stopper for the Halliards is fastned at the Main-Knight, and it serves when they are HoilingtheMain-Yard, to stop it, while the Men that Hale may stay and rest a little. But 'tis chiefly used for the Cable, to stop it, that it don’t run out too fast : They bind »hc Walc-kyiot about the Cable with the Larmiers, and that stops it, so that it cannot slip away. This Stopper is fastned to the .Bottom of the Pitts by the Heck. The Word is, Lay on the Stoppers. And a Ship is said to Rjde by the Stoppers, when the Cable is fastned or stayed only by them, and not Bitted ■ but this is nor safe Riding in a stress of Weather.

strike.c: STRIKE, a Sea-word variously used : When a Ship in a Fight, or on meeting with a Man of War, lets down or lowers her Top-fails, at least half Mast high, which they call Striking the Topsails upon the Bunt, they say, She Strikes, meaning, she Yields or Submits, or pays her Devoir to that Man of War as (be passes by. When any Top-mast is to be taken down, the Word is, Strike the Tep-mast : And when any thing is Let or Lowered, as they call it, down into the Hold, they call it Striking down into the Hold. subtraction.c: SUBTRACTION, in the general, is taking a. lesser Quantity from a greater, to find the Difference between them, which is commonly called the Remainder ; as the Lesser Quantity to be subtracted, is. called the Subtrahend. The General Sign or Mark of Subtraction is --- SUBTRACTION, in Algebra, or in Species, conjoyhs the Magnitudes proposed, changing all the Signs of the Subtrahend. Thus: If from 4 a, you Subtract a, by changing the Sign of the Subtrahend, it will stand thus, 4 a — a X = 3 St Or thus. 4 a — a — 1 a. And in Algebra, the Remainder, or Difference is usually noted by the Letter X, or d. N. B. To Subtract -\-, is the same as to add — and to Subtract —, is all one as to add -jj as is plain from the Reasons given in Addition in Algebra ; which see. Algcbraick Subtraction, in Compound Quantities, will easily be performed by only observing the General Rule of changing the Signs of the Quantity to be subtracted, and then comparing the several Members together, and contracting them. As suppose from 36 b -j5 mm -— 7 d f, you would Subtract 20 b -jids -j5 m m. Write them down one under another, changing all th* Signs of the Subtrahend; and it will stand thus. 36 b -j5 m m — 7 d f — 2o b — 5 mm — 2 df 16 b — 9, df =~X Which compared and contracted, will give the Difference or Remainder.

SUN, Our Excellent Mr. Isaac Newton faith in tos Principia, That the Density of the Sun's Light (which is Proportional to Heat) is seven times as Stoat in Mercury, as with us; and therefore our Water there, would all be carried off, and boil aw ay ; For he found by Experiments of the Thermo- *>tcter, That an Heat but 7 times as great as that of the Sun Beams in Summer, will serve to make w^ter boil. He Proves also, That the Matter of the Sun *■0 that of Jupiter, is nearly as Il 00 to l ; and .at the Distance of that Planet from the Sun, is ln the same Ratio to the Sun’s Sentidiameter. 1 hat the Matter of the Sun to that of Saturn, is to i ; and the Distance of Saturn from the bun, i s i n a Ratio, but a little less than that, to toe Sun’s Semidiamerer. And Consequently that the common Centre of gravity, of the Sun, and Jupiter j is nearly in the superficies of the Sun ; of Saturn, and the Sun a 'hie within st. And by the same manner of Cal- ^tohjdon, it will be found that the common Centre °i Gravity of all the Planets, cannot be more than toe Length of the Solar Diameter distant from the .»tre of the Sun : This common Centre of Grainy he proves to be at rest ; and therefore tho’ the un by reason of the various Position of the Planets ? a y be moved every way, yet it cannot recced ^ from that common Centre of Gravity. And ls he thinks ought to be accounted the Centre of Our World. Book. ■$.prop. tz. By Means of the Solar Spots st hath been difeototost that the Sun revolves round his own Axis, "hour moving (considerably ) out of his Place in bout 25 Days. And that the Axis of this MotijJ 1 ls enclined to the Ecliptick, in an Angle of 87 e grcces, 30 Minutes nearly. Grcgor. AJironom. « f be Sun’s apparent Diameter being sensibly 0rce £ in December than in June, as is plain and agreed from observation ; the Sun must be Proportionably nearer to the Earth in Winter than in Summer • in the former of which Seasons will be the Perihelion, in the latter the Aphelion: And this is also confirmed by the Earth’s moving swifter in December, than it doth in June j as it doth about T (. For since, as Mr, Newton hath demonstrated by a Line drawn to the Sun, the Earth always describes equal Area’s in equal Times, when ever it moves 1 writer, it must needs be nearer to the Sun. And for this Reason there are about 8 Days more from the Sun’s Vernal Equinox to the Autumnal, than from the Autumnal to the Vernal. According to Mr. Cafstni, the Sun’s greatest Distance from the Earth is 22374, his mean Distance 22000, and his least Distance 8022 Semi-diameters of the Earth. And that the Sun’s Diameter is equal to 100 Diameters of the Earth, and therefore the Body of the Sun, must be 1000000 times greater than that of the Earth. Mr. A^out assures us that he observed by a very exact Method the Sun’s Diameter to be not less than 31 Minutes, 45 Seconds in his Apogee, and not greater than 32 Minutes 45 Seconds in his Perigee. The mean Apparent Diameter of the Sun according to Mr. Newton, is 32 Minutes 12 Seconds, in his Theory of the Moon, 32' ist’. If you divide 360 Degrees (/ e the whole Ecliptick) by the Quantity of the Solar Year, st will Quote 5 9 Minutes, 8 Seconds, (sic. which therefore is the Quantity of the Sun’s Diurnal Motion. And if this 5 9 Minutes, 8 Seconds be divided by 24, you have the Sun’s Horary Motion, which is 2 Minutes, 28 Seconds, and if you will divide this last by 60, you will have his Motion in a Minute, (He. And this way are the Tables of the Sun’s mean Morion, which you have in the Books of Astronomical Calculation, constructed. The Sun’s Horizontal Parallax, Dr. Gregory (and Mr. Newton) makes but to Seconds. The same learned Mathematician, at the end of his Astronomies Physt. (H Geometr. Elem. hath a Comparative Astronomy, where among the rest he considers what Phenomena would appear in the Planetary System, (He. to an Eye placed at the Sun j which are such as these. , 1. That the Fixt Stars would appear in a Concave Sphere, the apparent Centre of which, is the Eye of the Spectator. 2. He would distinguish the Planets from the Fixt Stars (tho’ they would appear to him to be placed among them) by their Periodical Revolutions, and by the Time of those, one Planet from another : And he would judge that Planet to be farthest off’, whose Periodical Revolution was the longest; and so on in order for the rest, (He. 3. To this Solar Observer’s Eye, the Planets would appear always di ret, and never Stationary, nor Retrograde, as they do to an Eye at the Earth : And they would be found to return to the same Fixt Stars again at Periods of very disscrcnt lengths; and the Inferior Planets would sometimes cover she Superior ones. 4. If you suppose the Eye to be moved from the Centre of the Sun to its Surface, then by the Parallax of the Planets some better guess will be had of their Distances, than by the Observation of the different Velocity and Tardity of their Motion, could before be obtained: For to the Eye thus placed, the Earths Horizontal Parallax will be 16 Mi6 S 2 nutes,

S 11 N S 11 P miles, equal to the Sun’s Semi-diameter, and consequently sensible enough. That of Saturn, will lie something above one Minute and an half, (that Planet being i o times the Distance of the lirtrth stem the Sun ;) and the Horizontal Parallax of Mercury, will be almost 50 Minutes : And since these Parallaxes ate sufficiently sensible) the Distances of the Planets may be compared with the Sun’s Diameter, and with one another. 5. To an Eye thus placed all the Fixr Stars and Planets, will seem to revolve from East to Weft, in the Space of 15 of ourNatutal Days: The North Pole of which Revolution, will be in that part of the Heaven, which we (Inhabitants ol the Eaith) call the 10th Degree of Pijces, with 83 or 84 Degrees of North Latitude: Wherefore the Artick-Polc Star will beat the ad Flexure of Draco, and which will not be above 3 Degrees from the Pole. The South Pole will be in 10 Degrees of Virgo, with 8; or 84 Degrees South Latitude, near a Star of the fourth Magnitude, which in Cap. Ha Ik/s Catalogue, is in the first Oar of the Argo-Navis. 6 . The Planets thus seen from the Sun, will appear of Different Magnanitudcs : For the Diameter of Saturn, will subtend there but an Angle of 18 Seconds: That of Jupiter near 40 Seconds: That of Mars but 8 Seconds: That of Venus 2.8 Seconds : And the Diameter of Mercury 20 Seconds. But Ntt.Hugcns supposes the Diameters of the Superior Planets will be much larger ; as making that of Jupiter, to subtend an Angle of almost 54 Seconds; and that of the Body of Saturn without his Ring 27 Seconds. 7. Of these six Planets thus moving round the Sun, three will appear attended with their Satellites : Of which, the Earth will have but one, which is the Moon; and who will appear at the greatest distance, not to be from the Earth above 10 Minutes. Jupiter will appear with his four Moons, or Satellites ; of which the outermost will never appear to be above 9 Minutes distant from the Primary Planet. Saturn will appear with his 5 Satellites (if so many there be) and the furthermost of them will never be above 9 Minutes also distant from his Body : His Ring also will appear compassing round the Planet. The Paths, or Orbits of these Satellites being seen from the Sun sometimes more, sometimes lels Oblique, will appear accordingly now broader, now narrower Ellipses ; sometimes the Planes of these Orbits being produced, will pass thro’ the Sun : In which Case, the former narrow Ellipses will pass into Right Lines; which will happen twice in every Revolution of the Orbit round the Sun, if its Plane remain always parallel to it self: Whence the Satellite will now appear to be covered by the Primary Planet, and then the Planet by it; and sometimes will appear round the Planet, without its Disk, in an Ellipsis. 8. The Primary Planets, as also their Satellites, have not only rough and unpolished Surfaces, but also arc so difform, that they have their Spots, which arc places more or less obscure, (and sometimes more bright) than the rest of their Disk: And these Spots, by the Rotation of the Planet, or Satellite, round its Axis, do describe Circles ; and * therefore these Ways, or Paths of the Spots, being seen from the Sun in the Plane of the Planetary Disk, will now appear Elliptical, and now strait Lines, (as before the Paths of the Satellites Disk) according as the Sun is elevated on either side above the Plane of those Circles; or is found in lt > as it is when it is in the Equinoctial of that Planet. And if there be a Series, or Row, of these Spots, (as in the Belts of Mars and Jupiter) these wist appear in the form of Semi-Ehipscs (the one hast being behind, or on the other side the Planes) or will pass into strait Lines; which will also be the Case of the outward Edge of the Ring of Saturn. But Ionic of these Spots will now and then be hid, and sometimes be visible for a long time, according as they are near to the Planets Pole, which is turned from, or towards the Sun. .a nd this will be most observable in Saturn, and in the Eaith, in the others scarcely at all, because in them the Illustration of the Sun reaches to both their Poles. 9. Besides these six primary Planets, and the'* 1 o Satellites, which to our Solar Observatory wist all appear to move within the Bounds of a Zodiack, scarce 16 Degrees broad, and not much inclined to the Circle of the first Motion, all the same wap, and in Orbits nearly Concentrical to the Sun • There are also another kind of Bodies, whose Number is uncertain, which move round the Sun in very Eccentrical Orbits, and which are called Comets ; and which sometimes come very near the Sun, and sometimes are vastly remote from him. These Comets do not move all in the lame Track (altho’ each one always keeps his own) but som e one way, and some another, and mostly in Orbit 5 very much enc lined to the Ecliptick, and alway 5 in great Circles of the Sphere. Their Coma 01 Tail (to an Eye at the Sun) will not appear oblong, orstretcht out in length, as it doth to us, but every, way diffused round the Head.

sympatheticalinky.c:
SYMPATHETICAL Inky, are foch as can be made to appear or disappear very suddenly by the Application of something that seems to work by Sympathy. There are some ways of preparing Inks of this Kind ; which are really wonderful and surprising, as well as curious and diverting. The Experiments are these. Take of good unslacked Lime, two or three parts, according to the strength and goodness of the same, and one part of Yellow Orpiment, (which to powder, had best be wrapt up in a thick Paper, and so beaten, to prevent the dangerous Steams that may affect the Head) both these being powder’d and mixed, put to them 15 or 16 times as much Water, in Weight, as there was of Orpin : Stop the Viol well with Cork and a Bladder, and set it in warm Embers, or some such place ; soaking the Viol now and then for 4 or 5 Hours; then warily decant the clear part ; or which is better, filtrate it. In the mean time burn a piece of Cork throughly j and when it is well inflamed, quench it in common Water (or which is better, Atjua Vitrc, or Brandy) and by this means reducing ot it to a friable Coal, grind it with a fuifeient quantity of fair Water, in which you have dissolved a little GumArabic!^, and so it will make a Liquor as black as common Ink, which will serve very well to write any thing with. While these are doing, dissolve in three times as much distilled, or strong Vinegar, over warm Embers, a Quantity of fied Lead, (or Minium) ; or of Saccharum Saturn!, in three times as much Water, for 3 or 4 Hours, or till you find the Liquor have a very sweet Taste. This will likewise, as the first Liquor, be clear as common Water. All things being thus ready (for you must be pretty quick at it) write on a piece of Paper what you will, with this last Liquor, with a clean, or new Pen; and when it is dry, nothing will appear. Then over that place write with the Ink you made of the Cork, what you please; it will look just as if it had been written with common Ink, which let dry; then dipping a small piece of Rag, or a Sponge, in the first Liquor, rub it on the place written, and you will immediately fee the Black Writing vanish, and that written with the Invisible Ink, appear Black and Legible. Take also a Book 4 or 5 Inches thick, and writing on the first Blank Leaf with the last Liquor, or the Invisible Ink ; or j utting in there a Paper so written, turn to the other end of the Book, and rub there with a Rag dipt in the first Liquor, on that part that is as nearly as you can guess, oppo6 U r site

REASONS. sire to trie Writing, and leave also the Rag there : And over it clap a folded Paper, and nimbly slutting the Book, strik e 4 or 5 good Stroaks on it with your Hand, and then turning it t’other side uppermost, clap it into a Press, or lay it between two Boards with a-good Weight on it, for a quarter of an Hour (or half that time will do) then taking it out, you’ll find the Writing black and legible, which was written with the Invisible Ink. This Process, Mr. Boyle communicated in his History of Cold, fag. 3 22. and afterwards Lemery published it in his Course of Chymistry, with the Addition of the latter Experiment. By whole help we may endeavour at a Solution of these strange Experiments ; if we consider, 1. That the first of these Liquors is a mixture of the Alkalizate, and fiery Salt of Quick-lime, with the Sulphureous Substance of the Orpin, which is a kind of Arscnick.. 2. That the Blackness of the Ink, which is the second Liquor, proceeds only from the porous, light, and sooty parts of the Cork ; which are its Oily Parts very much ratified. 3. That the last Liquor (or the Invisible Ink) is only the Parts of the Lead held up imperceptibly in the acid Liquor of Vinegar. Hence then, the Reason of the disappearing of the Ink in the first Experiment, is from the penetrating Parts of the first Liquor, which consisting of an Alkalizate Salt, and a penetrating Oil, or Sulphur, doth make a kind of Soap, which soon dissolves the rarity’d Fulginosity of the Ink, as common Soap takes away grease Spots out of Cloaths, CV. And the Invisible Ink then appears black, because the Edges of the acid Liquor that hold the Parts of the Lead dissolved, being now broken by its Conflict with the Alkaly of the first Liquor; the Parts of the Lead, are, as it were, precipitated on the Paper, and so appear in their proper colour, which is Black. So that the Visible Ink disappears, because its Black Parts are dissolved ; and the Invisible doth appear, because it’s dissolved Parts are revived, or restored. The Second Experiment shews the strange piercing Subtil ty of the first Liquor. You had best make all the Liquors in different Places, least they should mingle, and so spoil the Experiment, as I have known them sometimes do. Experiment the Third. Dissolve a little White, or Green Vitriol in Water ; and then write with a clean Pen with the Solution, nothing will appear. Boil Galls in Water, and dip a Rag of Linnen in the Decoction, and with it rub the Place before written, and it will appear Black and Legible. But if you rub over it with a Feather, or a Rag dipt in Spirit of Vitriol, (or its Oil) the Letters will disappear again. Dip another Rag in Oil of Tartarpcr Deli qui am, and rub on the Place, the Letters will aspear again, but . of a Yellowish Colour. Lemery s Chymijlry, last Edit. fag. 33 b. The Coagulum of the Vitriol and Gab, is tj l1 Cause of the first Blackness, {as is seen in making common Ink.) which the acid Spirit of Vitriol dis solves, and so the Letters disappear: But the Oyl °J Tartar breaking (as it uses to do in all Precis it* 11 ' ons) the force of this acid Spirit, restores the Coagst lum ; but spoils its Colour a little, by mingling ,l self with it.

sympathetickpowder.c: SYMPATHETICK Powder, is only (said A** mery, Green, or Roman Vitriol, opened by the Sun Beams penetrating into it, and imperfectly calcining it: The Vitriol is usually exposed to the Sun s heat in the Month of July, but some use only P 0 "" der of Vitriol. When they use it, they spread so Ilie of the Powder upon a Lincn-cloth dipt in the Boodof any Wound, and then pretend, that if the Cloth be many Miles off the wounded Person, Y el he shall be healed : But this is so far from hew? true, notwithstanding the vaunting Stories of ^ Ken. Digby and others, That 'twill hardly have Effect if done in the same Room where the Patient lies ; and he certainly is very much wanting t0 himself, who will use no other help. Vitriol hath its Parts in continual Motion ; and ’tis probable, many Effluvia, may go out from > r » and some few of those, if the Application be mad c to the Cloth, just by the Patient, may perhaps enter into the Wound, and help stop the Bleedin?’ for Vitriol is a known Styptick ; but he that wi" neglect all other Means, and depend only on this, may probably pay dear for his Credulity. SYMPEPSlS, is a Coction of those Hum 01 ’ 5 * which are growing into an Impostume. ,

symphysis.c: SYMPHYSIS, is the joyning of two Bones, which neither has a proper distinct Motion : Th' 5 is either without any Medium, or else with it, aS with a Cartilage, or Grille, a Ligament, or Flest' £?c. ,

symptom.c: SYMPTOM, is a preternatural Disposition °; the Body, occasioned by some Disease ; this is c l' ther a Disease caused by another Disease ; or eh e the Cause of a Disease proceeding from’anoth^ Disease ; or else simply a Symptom : This last ' 5 either some Action of the Body hindred, or dist" r '. bed, some fault of the Excrement, or change the Natural Temper. Blanchard.

symptomaticalfevers.c: SYMPTOM ATICAL Fevers, according to son^' are those which arise from the Inflammation af» Putrefaction of Humors contained in some of th e Bowels, of which kind are those Fevers that accompany the Pleurisie, Inflammatiou of the Lung and Liver, Frengy, Quinste, and other Inflammations, or Ulcers of the Internal or External Parts.

synactica.c: SYNACTICA, arc Medicines that contract ans part.

synalpha.c: SYNALÆPHA, is a Figure in the Dimension, or Scanning of a Latine Verse ; whereby there 15 a Coalition of the two Vowels, or Dipthongs, orlC of which ends, and the other begins two con tig u ' ous Words in a Verse, so that they make hu c one.

synarthrosis.c: SYNARTHROSIS, is a joyning of Bones by a Grille, and is of two sorts vi^. Sutura, and Go” 1 ' phosis ; which see.

synchondrosis.c:
SYNCHONDROSIS, the same with Sy»« r ' thro its. SYNCHYS&

synchysis.c: SYNCHYSIS, in Grammar, is a confused and disorderly placing of Words in a Sentence.
SYNCHYSIS, a Disease, is a preternatural Confusion of the Blood, or Humors of the Eyes. Blanc hard.

syncopalisfebris.c: SYNCOPALIS Febris, or the Swooning Fever ; is that in which the Patient often Swoons and Faints a way. Blanchard.

syncopation.c: SYNCOPATION, a Term in Mustek, which is when a Note of one Part ends and breaks off upon the middle of a Note of another part.

syncope.c: SYNCOPE, in Mustek, is the driving a Note, when some shorter Note prefix’d at the beginning of the Measure, or Half-measure, is immediately follow’d by two, three, or more Notes of a greater Quantity, before you meet with another short Note equivalent to that which began the driving, to make the Number even. As when an odd Crotchet comes before two, three, or more Minims, or | an odd Quaver before two, three, or more Crotchets.
SYNCOPE, in Physick, is a sudden Prostration or Swooning, with a very weak, or no Pulse, and a Depravation of Sense and Motion.
SYNCOPE, in Grammar , is the taking away a Letter or Letters, out of the middle of a Word: As Dixti for Dixijti, Repostum for Repositum. SYNCRIT 1 CA. are relaxing Medicines.

syndesmus.c: SYNDESMUS, ox Syndcjmous, the same with a Ligament.

syndrome.c: SYNDROME, is a Concurrence of several Symptoms in the same Disease.

synecdoche.c: SYNECDOCHE, a Trope in Rlsetoriels, where the Name of the Whole is put for a Part; or the Name of the Part for the Whole : As if we should F.urope for England, or England for Europe. SYNECDOCHE, in Grammar, is when the Ablative Case of the Part, or the Adjunct, is changed into the Accusative: As in that of Virgil. Deiophobum vidi lacerum crude liter Ora. And in this: Flares inscripsi na minn. Begum. ■ .

synechphonesis.c: SYNECHPHONESIS, or Synthesis, is a Figure ! n Grammar, whereby two Vowels are contracted lnt o one as in this Verse of Virgil. &eu lento fuerint Alvearia vimina texta : ^hcrc the e<i in Alvearia, arc contracted into 0t >e Vowel.

synedrenonta.c: SYNEDRENONTA, are common Symptoms, r lc h accompany Diseases ; and yet neither stow Ut the Nature of the Disease, nor are necessary si -j. neo mitants of it; but do, notwithstanding, siges p Greatness, Continuance, tile. of the Di cynanche, is a sort of Squinancy, which Tute stopx the Breath; or a preternatural Instamof the Muscles of the Jaws. oYNeUROSIS, is an Articulation of Bones by pgatnent; as the Extremity of the Ulna, isjoinC ® ones °f the Carpus. p oYNGUL.TUS, the Hiccough, is a depraved ^vulsive Motion of the Stomach, by which it ^yours to expel something that is hurtful, or SYNlZESIS. See Syncchphonefis.

sinocha.c: I NOCHA, is a continued intermitting Fever; s "its for many Days with a great Hear, sometimes Putrefactions of the Blood: It is either Quotidian, Tertian, OX Quartan. Blancljrd.

synochus.c: SYNOCHUS, is a continued Fes er without any Intermission, or Abatement of the Heat, which continues for many Days: This is either simple, or accompanied with Putrefaction. Blanchard.

synod.c: SYNOD, A Meeting, or Assembly of Ecclesiastical Persons concerning Religion: Of which, there are four Kinds. i - General, where Bishops, &c. meet of all Nations. a. National, where those of one Nation only come together. j. A Provincial, where they of one only Province meet. 4. Diocesan, where those of but one Diocese meet: See Convocation, which is the same with Synod, only the one is a Greets, and the other a Latine Word. Cowc/’s Interpreter.

synodicalmonth.c: SYNODICAL Month, is the Space of Time,' {vi^. 29 Days, 12 Hours, 45 Minutes) contained between the Moon’s parting from the Sun at a Conjunction, and returning to him again j during which time, site puts on all her Phases. And her SYNODICAL Revolution, is that Motion whereby her whole System is carried along with the Earth round the Sun.

synonomy.c: SYNONOMY, is when the same thing is express’d by several Words that have but one and the lame signification : As if one should say, He went away, he escaped, he fled.

syntasis.c: SYNTASIS, is a preternatural Distension of the Parts.

syntectoe.c: SYNTECTOE, is a kind of Looseness that proceeds from the melting away of the Substance of the Body, by a violent hot Distemper of the solid Parts; such as sometimes happen in the Inflammation of the Bowels, and in a vehement burning Fever, Hectick, or Pestilential; in which a fat Matter, as it were mixt with Oil, or Grease, is voided by Stool.

syntenosts.c: SYNTENOSTS, is reckoned by some, to be the Unition of one Bone to another, by a Tendon ; as the Knee-pan to the Thigh-bone and Tibia.

synteretickmedicines.c: SYNTERETICK Medicines, are that part of Physick, which give Rules for the Preservation of Health.

syntaxis.c: SYNTHXIS, is a Consumption and Colligation of the Body, in which first the Flesh is wasted, and afterwards the Substance of the more solid Parts. Blanchard.

synthesis.c: SYNTHESIS, is either the Frame and Structure of the whole Body ; or more strictly, the Composure of the Bones. ’Tis also used in Mathematics, in opposition to the Word Analysts ; in which sense it signifies Composition, or the
SYNTHESIS is also used by the Grammarians, to signifie an Agreement of the Parts of a Sentence as to Sense, but not as to the Words. SYNULOSYS

syntheticalmethodofenquiry.c: SYNTHETICAL Method of Enquiry, or Demonstration in Mathematics, is when we pursue the Truth chiefly by Reasons drawn from Principles before established, and Propositions formerly proved, and proceed by a long regular Chain, till we come to the Conclusion : As is done in the Elements of Euclid, and in almost all the Demonstrations of the Ancients. This is called Composition, and is opposed to the Analytical Method, which is called Resolution ; which see.

synymensis.c: SYNYMENSIS, is taken to be the uniting of Bones together by a Membrane, as in Infants, the Bones of the Synciput, with the Os Frontis.

syphon.c: SYPHON, is a Tube, or Pipe of Glass, or Metal, which is usually bent to an Acute Angle, and having one Teg shorter than the other; they are frequently to draw off Liquors out of one Barrel, or Vessel, into another, without railing the Lees, or Dregs, and are called Cranes , Sometimes Glass Tubes, or Pipes, tho’ strait, are called Syphons. For the Cause of the running of Water, or other Liquors, through Syphons or Cranes See Hydrostatics, Paradox 10.

syringe.c: SYRINGE, is an Instrument which is used in injecting Liquors into Wounds, Ulcers, or any diseased Parts of the Body.

syringomat.c: SYRINGOMAT. 4 , are Chirurgcons Knives, which they open Fistula’s with.

syringotomia.c: SYRINGOTOMIA, is the Incision of the Fistula.

syssarcosis.c: SYSSARCOSIS, it the Connexion of Bones by Flesh. Blancbard,

system.c: SYSTEM, in Mustek, is the Extent of a certain Number of Chords, having its bounds toward the Grave and Acute, which hath been differently determin’d by the different Progress made in Mustek, and according to the different Divisions of the Momclmd. The System of the Ancients, was composed of four T etrachords, and one Supernumerary Chord, the whole making Fifteen Chords.

systemproperly.c: SYSTEM properly is a regular orderly Collection, or Composition of many things together. Thus the Solar System, is the Aggregate Union; or orderly Disposition of all thole Planets which move round the Sun as their Centre, in determined Orbits, and never deviate farther from him than their proper and usual Bounds. And a System of Philosophy, is a Regular Collection of the Principles and Parts of that Science into one Body, and a treating of them Dogmatically, or in a Scholaftical Method ; which is called the Systematical Way, in contra-distinction to the Way of Essay. , wherein the Writer delivers himself more loosely, easily, and modestly. The Learned Lr. Hook,, did in the Year 1674, at the end of his Attempt to prove the Motion of _ S Y Z _ I the Earth by Observation, promise that he would explain a System of die World, differing in many things from any then known, and yet exactly a ' greeable to Mechanical Principles. Which System he there says, depends on these three Suppositions, vi%. First, That all the Heavenly Bodies have a gravitating or attracting Power towards their own Centres, whereby they attract not only their own Parts, and keep them from flying off from thew, but also all other Celestial Bodies within the Sphere of their Activity. Secondly, That all Bodies put into a direct and simple Motion, will so continue to move forwards in a strait Line, till they are by some other more effectual Power bent or deflected into a Motion, which describes some Curve Line. Thirdly, That these attractive Powers are much the more powerful in operating by how much the nearer the Body wrought upon, is to their own Centres. All which is abundantly confirmed in Mr. lfi 4C Newton's Admirable Principia Philosophic Mat bent" tica.

systole.c: SYSTOLE, in Anatomy, is the Contraction ok the Ventricles of the Heart, whereby the Blood 15 forcibly driven into the great Artery. ,
SYSTOLE, in Grammar, is part of the Poetical Licence, whereby a long Syllable is made short* As in that os Virgil. * - T user sunt fasti dia Menses.

systyle.c: SYSTYLE, in ArchiteFlure, is a Building where the Pillars stand thick, but not alt jgether ib close as in the Pychnostyle; the Intcr-columniation, or Instance between them, being only two Diameter 5 of the Column.

syzygie.c:
SYZYGIE, in Astronomy, is the same with the Conjunction of any two Planets, or Stars, or when they are both referred to the same Point in the Heavens ; or when they are referred to the lame Degree of the Ecliptick, by a Circle of Longitude passing through them both. T A 0

But if there be an Interruption, that part which is separated from the other two, is called The middle part, and the other two arc Extreams opposite, or dijjunct.
